Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36(8), I have the honour to table, in both official languages, the government's response to eight petitions numbered as follows: 5484, 5488, 5489, 5490, 5532, 5560, 5627, 5651.
[Editor's Note: See today's Votes and Proceedings.]

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to present a petition on behalf of a number of constituents from Kamloops concerning the government's goods and services tax that is now before the Liberal Senate.
They are asking that the tax be stopped. They point out a whole set of reasons why they feel it ought to be stopped. One of the reasons is that it taxes reading, which makes Canada the only country in the world that does so.
They call upon the Liberals in the Senate to stop the tax.

Mr. Speaker, on another matter I have a petition to present from a number of western Canadians who point out the benefits to a country the size of Canada having a first class passenger rail service.
They also point out that all large countries like Canada have first class passenger rail service which is the most environmentally friendly way to travel.
They are urging the government to reconsider its decision to abandon a good part of the VIA system in the country.

Mr. Speaker, on a third matter I have a petition to present from petitioners who point out the increasing number of Canadian children who find themselves living in poverty. They point out that the number is actually increasing during these trying economic times for many families.
They are asking that the government support the initiative first introduced by the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam calling for a comprehensive bill of rights for children in Canada and to implement policies and take initiatives that would ensure that Canadian children cease living in poverty.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition certified correct under the Standing Orders. It is from a number of my constituents who are calling on the government again to save the VIA Rail system.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Walker (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speechtext:
That this House reaffirm that all persons are equal under the law and demand that the government (1) promote this fundamental human right for Canada's aboriginal peoples, (2) ensure that our system of justice is more responsive and suitable, (3) pursue alternative aboriginal justice initiatives, and (4) in cases of jurisdictional conflict, that the Government of Canada, in consultation with aboriginal leaders, ensure the protection of the life, liberty, and security of aboriginal people who are entitled to the status of Canadian citizens.
He said: Mr. Speaker, thank you for this opportunity to consider my motion.
It is time to lay out for the people of Canada in detail the extent to which the plight of our aboriginal peoples has become a national tragedy. Today, I only want to deal with one aspect of this tragedy, the question of human rights and our Canadian society.
As Canadians we have long pointed our fingers at others, and for good reason. The stories of El Salvador, Iran, Nepal, China and the Soviet Union, to mention
May 1, 1990

only a few, have brought senseless grief to millions. We have a right and an obligation to speak out as a democratic society in an undemocratic world.
With that privilege also comes an obligation. That obligation is to put our own house in order, to ensure that every Canadian is looked after in the spirit of a truly democratic society, and to ensure that this spirit is present in the structure of our judicial system, in the daily application of our laws, in the operation of our governments and in the political system itself.
We must give substance to our Charter of Rights which guarantees that:
Every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.
Sometimes these words have to be read in the House to remind ourselves as to what our obligations are as representatives of Canadians.
It is finally dawning on all Canadians that words are not enough. We are losing our way, and nothing shows our lack of commitment more than the way we treat this country's aboriginal peoples.
This motion is not based on my own opinion, but on the research, views and analyses of every individual, committee and commission that has looked into the critical problems facing our aboriginal peoples.
We are using this opposition day to request that the government show some understanding, some sympathy and some concrete movement in reaching out to these Canadians, and to recognize that the experience of aboriginal peoples is the dark side of our reality. We are bringing these issues forward so that we can leave behind the stage of denial and compel the Government of Canada to show good faith to the world. The aboriginal peoples are, after all, our people, and should be our friends and neighbours.
The law, and in many respects we have to say bluntly, the white man's law, has been unkind to Canadian aboriginal peoples. Throughout much of our history the law, like a two-edged sword, has denied natives the freedom to exercise the fundamental prerogatives of their ancestors and the Europeans who occupied their lands.
Supply
In the years which followed Confederation, one province after another enacted legislation which excluded natives from the franchise. In 1875, for example, British Columbia decreed that "no Chinaman or Indian" could vote, a provision which was upheld by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the highest court in the British Empire. Quebec, the last province to repeal its discriminatory legislation, only did so in 1969.
On the federal level, aboriginal peoples were also barred from participating in the electoral life of their country, a ban which was not lifted unconditionally until 1960. Not until 1972, it appears, did an aboriginal sit on a Canadian jury. The names of such individuals had been hitherto omitted from the list of potential jurors.
The list goes on and on as to how history has been an unfair weapon against our aboriginal peoples. But if you look at the situation currently, Mr. Speaker, you will see that we have not changed.
I would like to review some of the major findings that people have made concerning certain conditions of Canadian aboriginal peoples. The 1989 annual report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission repeats again the findings that it brought to the attention of Canadians in 1988.
In 1988, the commission stated that the justice system is heavily weighted against Canadian native peoples. It also stated that an Indian youngster in Canada has a better chance of being sent to prison than of completing university.
The commission argued that ways must be found to remove bias and to dispel the views of some natives that the justice system is "white law".
When the commissioner wrote his report this year, he came to the same conclusion as he came to in 1988. This time he said:
If there is any single issue on which Canada cannot hold its head
high in the international community, any single area in which we can
be accused of falling down on our obligations, it is in this area of
aboriginal relations.
In his frustration in trying to get the Government of Canada to act this time he recommended the creation of a royal commission. That recommendation is still before the government.

May 1, 1990
Supply
This year, an interdepartmental committee finished its review of Indian policing policy. This report states that "Indian communities are entitled to effective and culturally sensitive law enforcement services" which should be of the same standard as those enjoyed by similarly situated non-native communities.
It also states that Indians can "legitimately expect to increase their control over their own future and be policed increasingly by Indians," regardless of the policing program which is serving them.
The statistics that the committee presents indicate that the average number of on-reserve crimes per thousand is approximately four times the national average.
Reserves which are served by regular police programs suffer from problems of slow response time, little to no preventive policing work, no enforcement of band bylaws and poor communications between the band, its membership and the regular police serving the reserve. So far the government has not taken any action on this task force report.
I would like to refer now to the final report of the Task Force on Aboriginal Peoples in Federal Corrections. This was a task force created in 1987, which reported in 1989, to find ways to improve the treatment of aboriginal peoples in the federal corrections system. It stated that the need for improvement was demonstrated by the fact that aboriginal people comprise 2.5 per cent of the Canadian population but a full 9 per cent of federal inmates.
Also, fewer aboriginal people are granted full parole, and when it comes it is later in their sentences, and they are more likely to have their parole revoked.
The task force made more than 60 recommendations touching every aspect of the corrections system as it relates to aboriginal offenders. These include recommendations such as having increased aboriginal correctional staff, working with aboriginal communities and organizations so that they be better informed and involved with the delivery of programs and that the institutional environment provide further support to aboriginal culture, spiritual values by, for example, improving the access of aboriginal elders to correctional institutions.
The task force emphasized that in judging the performance of aboriginal inmates it was important to understand the social and cultural realities of aboriginal life, otherwise discrimination in the treatment of aboriginal offenders would be certain to continue.
More recently, and I think perhaps more important because it brings home the message to all of us, was the 1990 report from the fask Force on Federally Sentenced Women. Eight emergency measure recommendations were made. A number made specific mention of aboriginal inmates.
One of the major concerns that we have in this country is the fact that not only is there a high rate of incarceration among aboriginals in general, it is even higher among women. Their problems are compounded by the fact that the prisons available to them take them away from their community life and take them away from their family support systems. Many end up in Prince Albert or, on occasion, they are brought east to Kingston. Most of these people originate in western Canada, far removed from Kingston.
Once cut off from these services the likelihood of being able to return to a productive life back home on a reserve or in urban centres that they come from is near impossible. The fact is that the government has failed to recognize that the issue of women in prisons is largely at this time an issue of aboriginal women in prison and that it needs to be addressed immediately.
It is not only the federal government which has been reporting on the problems facing aboriginal peoples in Canada in dealing with human rights issues, but also provincial governments. For example, as this debate takes place, there is a task force in Alberta reviewing the judicial system there.
There is also a judicial review in Manitoba which is coming to its conclusion. Hopefully, its report, which is coming out shortly, will add and contribute positively to the debate.
In Nova Scotia last year we heard from the Royal Commission on Donald Marshall. This report will be referred to in more detail by one of my colleagues who finds it particularly oppressive. She will bring the report to the attention of the House in more detail.
For now, it is important to point out that this Royal Commission concluded that Mr. Marshall's race was a factor in his wrongful conviction and 11-year incarceration for the murder of Sandy Seale. It found that the
May 1, 1990

judicial system failed Marshall at virtually every turn from his arrest and conviction in 1971 up to and beyond his acquittal by the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia.
It found that the individuals involved in the judicial system failed to perform their duties in a professional and/or competent manner, thereby allowing this tragedy to happen.
In 1988, the Canadian Bar Association turned its attention to aboriginal peoples and cited in its report, called Locking up Natives in Canada, a Saskatchewan study that shows that a treaty Indian male who turned 16 in 1976 had a 70 per cent chance of at least one stint in prison by the age of 25. For a non-native, this figure was 8 per cent-70 per cent versus 8 per cent. That is almost a factor of 10. Again, it draws to our attention the dramatic difference in the lifestyle and problems that aboriginal youth run into compared to non-aboriginal youth.
Some of the grim statistics the report reviewed show that infant mortality among Indian children was 60 per cent higher than the figure for the country as a whole. These are figures that you read about normally concerning Third World countries. If there is anything that hits at the heart of human rights and why the UN has turned its attention to human rights, it is the treatment of children. The fact that we have an infant mortality rate in Canada so much higher for this particular group again points out one of the many ways we are failing these people.
Indian children who survive their first year of life can expect to die ten years before their non-native contemporaries. The rate of violent death among Indians is more than three'times the national average. The likelihood of Indian minors being placed in the custody of a child welfare agency is five times higher than that for non-native children.
The Bar Association concluded that what we need in Canada is a criminal justice system which does more than respond to dispossession and deprivation by locking up natives. This again shows the frustration not only of people in government, not only of people in the communities themselves, but very much of people such as
Supply
lawyers and judges who are looking at these people on a daily basis wishing that another system could be set up.
The Bar Association came up with an idea which is gaining currency in Canada. It is one that I think the House should look at. I refer to an alternative native justice system. Members of the committee of the Bar Association believe that there is a sound constitutional basis for them. Although they refrain from endorsing a particular model, they feel that these systems could reflect the accumulated wisdom of both aboriginal law ways and the common law. I think it is time that the government begins to look at the alternative legal systems being tried in the United States and being suggested by different inquiries throughout Canada.
Perhaps one of the most moving ways of looking at the issue of native people and the law was offered by a reporter, Geoffrey York, of The Globe and Mail who has just published a book called The Dispossessed. In using his experience, mostly throughout western Canada, he went to different communities and talked to the leadership and people in different communities about native issues. He stated that for many native youths the reformatory is more attractive than life on the reserve, that incarceration provides a welcome escape from isolation, poverty and boredom.
He quotes one young aboriginal person who said of his peers:
We have nothing to look forward to when we wake up in the morning. We get frustrated and scared. We don't give a damn what happens to anybody any more because nobody gives a damn about us. The only thing we know is to cause trouble and go to jail, where you have three meals a day and a place to sleep and a TV to look at.
I cannot think of a more incriminating commentary on the situation we have created, and everyone is responsible, than to think of people who see their life as one in which going to jail is the only alternative because they cannot work productively in their community.
However, many communities are trying to take the initiative to improve their lot, with or without the support of the government. In 1987, for example, crime rates fell significantly in four native communities in northern Manitoba after a sports and recreation program was instituted for the inhabitants.
It is hard to believe that when the government built some of the reserve infrastructure it did not bother to build sports and recreation facilities on these reserves. So the youth had no place to go. Even the schools often

May 1, 1990
Supply
have very limited facilities. During the long winter periods in remote communities people get more and more frustrated. A simple thing like a physical infrastructure would make it possible for them to live a more positive lifestyle.
Prince Albert is very well known for its prisons in western Canada. There are in fact three facilities, and each is filled with natives. The population of the federal penitentiary is 50 per cent native, the population of the provincial correctional centre is 75 per cent native and the population of the women's jail is 85 per cent native.
It is obviously easy to spend all day going through statistics and reports, but I think the point is well made that no matter who looks at the Canadian system, whether it is the United Nations which has sent an observer into western Canada, whether it is the South African ambassador who took the opportunity to embarrass Canadians by visiting a reserve in central Manitoba, whether it is a departmental committee, whether it is the Human Rights Commission, whether it is a provincial royal commission or whether it is a judicial study in Manitoba or Alberta, everyone comes to the same conclusion. The human rights of Canadian aboriginal people are being put at risk by one generation after another of Canadians who fail to come to grips with this problem, who fail to recognize that they must do something, and begin now.
This is an opportunity and an obligation on the part of the government. This is not something that people come to do easily in their communities. Anyone who thinks that out of local goodness people will begin to look at the problems of aboriginals, is walking away from his or her own responsibility as federal leaders. People need to see that the government itself is willing to stand up and protect people. They need to see that there will be programs which respond to people. People living in Norway House or in Shamattawa want to know the government is willing to come up and say: "Here is a facility for you. Here is a local police program. Here is an opportunity for you to join in crime prevention. Here is an opportunity for you to protect your own human rights."
People look to the federal government as the heart of liberal values in this country. One of the reasons why we
have tried to develop a strong federal government in Canada, going back to the turn of the century, is that it has become the focus for human rights battles. This is where we develop law.
This is where we develop the interpretation of laws, through the federal government and through the federal court system. This is why we provide money through the Court Challenges Program. This is why we have provided for the education of the RCMP. This takes place at the federal level, and therefore I call upon the government today to think about its inactivity, to think about the fact that it is not taking these initiatives.
In the meantime, people are going to jail at the age of 16. Family violence is on the increase. People are having difficulty developing a positive lifestyle. In the the absence of action on the human rights questions, we once again have failed many people.
This motion has four components to it. Each one of them asks the government to consider different approaches: promoting equality; ensuring that our system of justice is more responsive and suitable; and pursuing alternative aboriginal justice initiatives. These three components, plus the fourth component which deals more specifically with the problem to be addressed by the next speaker, are very straight forward. There is nothing complicated about asking the government to act immediately.

speakeroldname: Hon. Shirley Martin (Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate today.
Yesterday, I had an experience that was both saddening and uplifting as I visited the families, mainly the elderly, women and children, who have been forced from their traditional lands by a small group of violent people trying to impose their wishes by force of arms. We have all heard on the radio, seen on television and in the newspapers, the report about the critical situation at the St. Regis Akwesasne Reserve.
I know that members on all sides of this House realize that what is happening in this native community is extremely complex. The current difficulties have been brewing for some time. Informed people understand that there is no easy, quick solution to a problem involving five governments, the governments of Canada, Quebec, Ontario, the State of New York, the United States of

May 1, 1990

America and the Mohawk people on both sides of the border.
Not the least of the complications is the fact that the community of St. Regis, part of the reserve, is Canadian territory but is physically cut off from the rest of Canada by the St. Lawrence River and the St. Regis River and the United States border. This explains why the Surete du Quebec evacuated many residents of St. Regis by boat last Friday. This unusual move was necessary because the normal route by road was controlled by members of the Mohawk Warrior Society, a group based on the American side.
I think it would be helpful to review briefly the events of the last few days to gain a better understanding of the current situation. On Wednesday my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and myself met with several native leaders, including George Erasmus the national Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, Mr. Harry Laforme who is the Indian Commissioner of Ontario, Grand Chief Mike Mitchell of the Akwesasne Community, Chief Harold Tarbell who is Head Chief of the St. Regis Tribal Council, and Tom Porter, Chief of the Traditional Council.
The same night and the following day we consulted with the Attorney General of Ontario and the office of the Minister of Public Safety in Quebec.
Early Friday morning, following several days of violent clashes, the band decided to evacuate the St. Regis Reserve and sought the help of the Quebec police force to move its people to safety. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Ontario Provincial Police provided assistance, including boats, to the Surete du Quebec who co-ordinated the operation to ensure the protection of the persons evacuated.
Approximately 600 persons registered at the Transport Canada Training Institute in Cornwall and the evacuees were accommodated there. For those who do not know the training centre, it is a school-room and hotel-like atmosphere where students who are being trained by Transport Canada normally stay.
Some of those evacuated wanted to return to protect their homes but Grand Chief Mike Mitchell has convinced most of the band members to remain in Cornwall for their own safety.
Supply
At a meeting on Saturday morning, the community discussed what they might do regarding a return to their homes. As we can all understand, they were most anxious about their homes, now empty and unprotected from possible attack. The group decided to stay in Cornwall and postpone their return to the reserve.
Chief Mike Mitchell, Chief Harold Tarbell and Chief Tom Porter thanked the city of Cornwall and the Canadian government for their assistance and called once again for American intervention. I would like to join them and express my sincere appreciation for the co-operation and assistance of those who participated in this commendable effort.
Mr. Speaker, I think Parliament can take satisfaction in the actions of the government in assisting those men, women and children that sought refuge in Cornwall. The Transport Canada Training Institute provided food and shelter for those who did not feel safe on the reserve.
In fact, when I was there yesterday they were showing me the food that had come in from the community, from the people in Cornwall-everything from disposable diapers, to food, to toys for the children. It really was rewarding to see how the city of Cornwall responded to this situation and helped these unfortunate people.
Officials from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are there now and have been throughout the evacuation period to provide whatever help and reassurance necessary to our native people.
When I travelled to Cornwall yesterday and met with the St. Regis Band members there, I must say I was deeply moved by the fear, which was mixed with courage and determination not to submit to the scare tactics that threaten their community and their way of life.
Our objective is to strive for a peaceful solution, acceptable to all sides. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has explained to the House that he has made representations to the Secretary of State of the United States. He has told his American counterpart that we have a situation that is near anarchy; that much of the source of the problem is on the American side; and that we urge response by American authorities, particularly those from the State of New York.

May 1, 1990
Supply
The government has shown its determination to play an effective role in bringing about a peaceful resolution. We expect the Americans, both at the state and national level, to act promptly to resolve the situation.
In its actions over the last few days, our government has demonstrated its commitment to protecting the interests of all Canadians and all aboriginal peoples. No one in this House accepts the idea that native people in this country can be forced from their homes by a violent and illegal action of a small group from another country, even if that country is our good neighbour, the United States of America.
Canada has a different history with respect to resolving conflict than those of our American cousins. We have a tradition and a Constitution which emphasizes negotiation, not confrontation.
The hon. members across the floor, and our own members, may grow impatient with our desire to find a solution which is both peaceful and lasting, but that is a non-violent approach which contributes to a high reputation in this world as a nation of peace-keepers.
Personally, I am proud of this history of treaty-making and peaceful negotiations which has characterized our approach in resolving our relationship with native people. This does not mean that there is not room for further improvement. The Marshall inquiry and other continuing inquiries have shown us that justice is a matter for every responsible person, and it is an institution which must strive continually to obtain goals of justice and freedom.
The most recent events in Akwesasne show that Canada should continue to strive for a land where all citizens have access to peace and freedom. We must have order and peace so we can reach that freedom, not reach it through violence. Most importantly, in full respect of their honour and dignity to deserve its high reputation as a leader among nations, as Canadians we must strive continually for justice for all.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for her measured speech this morning. I appreciate her comments. I know she was at Akwesasne yesterday, or near Akwesasne, I should say. I would not blame her for not going there right now. I would not either, even though
part of the reserve is in my riding. I would not go there now out of fear for my own safety, and besides I would not want to cause tempers to flare any higher than they are at the present time. I am sure that is the case for the minister, as well.
We will be discussing this subject today and tomorrow, and hopefully finding a resolution to a very difficult problem. I want to make one or two suggestions.
I notice the Solicitor General is here and I welcome his presence. Whatever means we find must be utilized to disarm the community. This is what will have to be done. I do not think there is any question that efforts will have to be made on both sides of the border simultaneously. I do not want the minister to give me any great detail on how that is going to be done because, obviously, it will have to be done in certain confidence that all police forces approach this at the same time.
My concern is that the village of St. Regis is on Canadian soil but only accessible through the United States, as the minister has indicated. Perhaps for some members, that may be a little hard to figure out. One would almost need a map of the area, as a prop, to show members the configuration of the reserve, so that everyone would understand what we are talking about. Of course, we cannot do that in this House. I only say that to illustrate how complicated the border is.
I want to return to the remarks I was making and suggest to the minister that efforts be made on both the Canadian and the U.S. sides with the police forces in order to disarm the community. It is important that it be done simultaneously simply because, if we are talking about the community of St. Regis and the United States, there is no Customs officers there.
Perhaps the two ministers have not been to that part of the reserve. Our distinguished colleague from Beauhar-nois-Salaberry and I have been there on a number of occasions. There are no customs. It is actually the only place in Canada where you can legally cross between Canada and the United States without going through customs. There is actually such a place in Canada. It is Akwesasne. Strangely enough, if you go between Cornwall Island in Akwesasne and the U.S. side you have to pass through customs, but if you go from St. Regis to the U.S. side there is no such thing as a customs office. My fear, of course, would be that the guns and everything else would just move across the border if whatever is
May 1, 1990

done is not done simultaneously on both sides. That is the first concern.
I have discussed the second point privately with the Solicitor General. It is my hope that once everything is solved, we will find a way to build a road or a bridge-it will have to be a combination of a road and a bridge- between the village of St. Regis and the village of Snye. Both villages are on the Quebec side of the Akwesasne Reserve but one is separated from the other by a body of water, as the minister has indicated. By constructing this access-and I hope it is done on an urgent basis and hopefully this year in a combination between the Government of Canada and the Government of Quebec-it would ensure that the people of St. Regis are never landlocked again and are never put in a situation where they become hostages in their own village. That is unique to Akwesasne and it is something which is certainly undesirable. We are seeing now that our citizens can be landlocked in that manner and dependent on the level of law and order in another country for their safety.
I will have several other remarks to make later when I make my own speech but I would like to raise one of my concerns. I do not expect a response to the first one as it is probably better that there is no response other than an acknowledgement of the concern.
On the second one, I would hope that I could get a commitment from the government that there would be high level negotiations with Quebec in order to build such a road and bridge between those two Canadian communities so that they are no longer landlocked and potentially held hostage, as we have seen over the last few days.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his comments on this issue. I know it is one that he has a great interest in because we have had personal conversations as this has been going on.
I thank you for the suggestion about the bridge because it is very unique and it is hard for people to understand. It would be as if we, sitting here in the House, to get to our office in Hull had to go out the back door and climb into a boat to go across the river in order to get there. That the reserve is in Ontario, Quebec and the United States is a very unique situation and there is not a continuous method of transportation between them.
Supply
As far as the disarming is concerned, I agree with the hon. member. This is not something that can take place unilaterally by any part of the reserve. It must be done in unison. If we are to attain a peaceful solution, the arms must be laid down. People cannot live in fear of their lives because of shots being fired, and even though they may be only fired in the air, it is still a method of intimidation and fear. It is very important that those arms be laid down.
I do not know of any place in the world where peace has been obtained and solutions have been found under gunfire. In all cases the guns have been laid aside and then negotiations and mediation have taken place. I feel that this is what has to happen at Akwesasne. As most of the guns and certainly the majority of the firing has come from the American side, it is very important that we have the co-operation of the United States and the State of New York in order to obtain this.
In fact, as we are debating this matter in the House, there is a meeting going on between the officials in the Department of Indian Affairs in Canada, the bureau of Indian Affairs in the United States, representatives from the State of New York and from External Affairs and from Washington. These officials are discussing opportunities for a peaceful solution to this particular situation. I am looking forward to the results of that meeting. We may not have an immediate solution based on the meeting this morning but it is a first step in the right direction, the bringing together of both sides to try and obtain a solution.
The problem belongs to Akwesasne. It is the people of Akwesasne who must face the issue of the gambling that is taking place. It is something they have to solve among themselves. However we, as the government of Canada, with the provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec, as well as the American government, must do what we can to help facilitate the groups to come together and to forge a peaceful solution to the problems they have there.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the funding of native Canadians comes from many sources within this government, primarily through my department, the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs. In fact, the budget for my department was increased by some 8 per cent this year to ensure that the necessary funding to provide the services to the native people that are required, whether it be in education, in health, or in infrastructure within their reserves, has been increased because we realize that the need is there.
Native people have been making great strides in education. There is a long way to go but there has been much growth in the number of people going into post-secondary education and post-elementary education over the last four to five years and I hope to see that continue to grow.
While there were some cut-backs in the over-all budget of the Secretary of State, and some of those cuts were reflected back within the native people, there is also a committee put together to look for other ways of funding those communication areas for the native people. Money will come from other sources and be on a more ongoing basis to allow them to continue with their communications. But certainly the over-all budget as far as aboriginal and native people in Canada are concerned has been increased and will continue to be funded at levels where we can continue to work with the native people.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member for Winnipeg North Centre for presenting this motion and raising this issue in the House today, and also for his comments on how native Indians relate to the justice system in Canada and
some of the problems that he has outlined in his comments.
Also, I appreciate that the Minister of State would want to confine her remarks to the current problems at Akwesasne. I think all that we on this side, in this party, would like to say is that we appreciate that this matter is being treated sensitively and that we would not like to see the kind of violence that has taken place over the past few days increase. We appreciate the fact that there is an attempt being made to bring the parties together to negotiate a resolution to this issue rather than to follow the suggestions of some people that, for example, the National Guard be brought in to deal with the issue. I think that that kind of response would probably beget more violence and not bring about the kind of solution that we would like to see. I appreciate the Minister of State's approach, which is to bring the parties together to negotiate a resolution and then to see what can be done, respecting the views of all the parties involved, and also respecting the issue of Mohawk sovereignty over their lands which is an important issue.
I would like to discuss some of the broader issues relating to native justice in this country, not simply the Akwesasne issue or the issue of the justice inquiries that were brought up by the member for Winnipeg North Centre.
The problem of natives in conflict with the justice system, as offenders, is only the tip of the iceberg in this country. The evidence is overwhelming that natives are not well treated by the justice system in Canada. The member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned the Donald Marshall inquiry and the statement in the Marshall inquiry that if it was not for his race, Donald Marshall would not have been considered the prime suspect in this case, and would not have gone to jail for years and years as a result of the ineffectiveness of the courts, the police and the whole justice system.
I am pleased to see that there are now inquiries taking place, in both Manitoba and Alberta, into instances that have emphasized how unjustly natives are treated in those provinces. It is a fact I think we are all aware of, that in Manitoba federal prisons, 39 per cent of the inmates are native, even though natives make up only about 2 per cent of the population. In Saskatchewan, 36 per cent of inmates are natives, although natives make up only about 2 per cent of the population. The provincial prisons in both of those provinces and across Canada show a disproportionate number of native inmates incar-
May 1, 1990

cerated in correctional institutions as a result of the problems that the justice system has in dealing with native people.
I think we should recognize the work of the Human Rights Commissioner over the last two years and the Canadian Bar Association and other authorities who have dealt with this issue and who have tried to work with the Canadian government to develop changes to the problems of native justice in this country. I think their work, hopefully, will lead to some resolution of this problem.
The government, at this point, seems to have taken the position that our justice system is fine but it needs a few refinements in order to accommodate native Indians in Canada. I do not think that that response or that reaction goes far enough. I think we have to look at the roots of this problem and that the solutions we come up with and that ultimately will be successful are going to be far more radical and more far-reaching than the solutions that seem to be acceptable to the government at this time.
Native injustice does not simply begin when native offenders come into conflict with the laws of the dominant society. The injustice has been present over the last 200 years. It begins with the status to which we assign native people in this country, through our laws, through the way we administer the Department of Indian Affairs, and, essentially, the role of native people in this country is the role of colonized people virtually anywhere in the world. They have been pushed to the margins of society, they are treated as colonized people and we, who supposedly represent the dominant society, are the colonizers. The problem with the relationship is that native society has been relegated to the margins and relegated to the status of lesser importance. The treatment, as far as I am concerned, of native people in this country is no different, except perhaps in terms of degree than the treatment of the Congolese during the colonial period in the Belgian Congo. The colonized people were marginalized, were seen as secondary people and in fact in many cases, non-people relative to the dominant colonizing society and I do not think that that is any different in Canada. When you start by looking at the references to native people in our fundamental constitutional documents, there is absolutely no way that our constitutional documents recognize the role that
Supply
native people played in our country prior to the period of colonization when the European and other people came here.
Our constitutional documents do not give adequate mention to the role and the importance of native people in our society. I suppose, with the exceptions in the British North America Act that assigned jurisdiction of natives and lands reserved for natives to the federal government or some mention in the Constitution Act of 1982 that existing aboriginal rights and treaties will be respected, there is very little in the constitutional documents that recognize the importance of the role that native people have played and should be playing in our country today.
Today we seem to be locked in with the Meech Lake discussions in a discussion around who are the founding nations of this country, how they should be mentioned or displayed in our constitutional documents, and what rights and privileges should be assigned to them.
Yet it is strange that one of the fundamental characteristics of this country was that we as colonizers found people here when we arrived. These people had organized societies, they had their own governments, they had ways of managing the land, they had ways of allocating property, and they had the power in their governments to both make war and to make treaties of peace. In fact, every characteristic that is a fundamental characteristic of a nation was enjoyed by those nations of aboriginal people our forefathers and mothers found when they arrived on these shores hundreds of years ago. Those nations also had their economies and their trade relationships with other nations.
Any characteristic or right of a nation that would have the right to be a member of the United Nations today or the right to participate in national debates throughout the world were present in those nations that we found here in the beginning. Even the colonizers who came here took advantage of some of those characteristics by entering into treaties with those nations, as if they were sovereign people and recognizing that they were sovereign people in their own lands. They signed treaties of peace. They signed alliances in times of war when the European colonizers fought against each other. In fact, they were treated in the early history of our country as

May 1, 1990
Supply
sovereign nations, but something has happened in the meantime. We have forgotten those treaties. We have forgotten the sovereignty that has to be recognized prior to entering into a treaty with the people we found here and we have now forced those people to the margins. In fact, we have begun to treat them as non-people.
It might be worth while, when talking about the injustice that is meted out to native Indian people by our country, to look at some of the fundamental documents of legislation by which this injustice is institutionalized in the way this Parliament operates and in the way the federal government administration operates.
One is the issue of the assignment of status as native Indians. One of the primary tenets of culture is that a culture recruits its own members and has the right to recruit its own members. Native Indians should be deciding who are Indians and who are not, and I think that they would find it relatively easy to do that.
Instead, we have arrogated that right to ourselves here in Parliament. For example, we had decided that if a native woman marries outside her race, then she loses her Indian status. We made that decision right here in this Parliament. We decided right here in this Parliament that if a native decided to join the Canadian Forces and fight for this country during the war, that in the very process of doing that, he lost his status as an Indian. What other group in this country loses their cultural status by joining the Canadian Armed Forces, and yet we forced native Indians to go through that process of being enfranchised in order to fight for this country.
Some months ago in the House I brought up the incident of the Stoney Point base in southern Ontario, where we had examples of the Canadian army seizing a native reserve as a military base and promising to return it after the war. Some of the men on that military base signed up in the Canadian army, lost their Indian status, and when they came home after the war they found that they had lost the homes for which they fought because the Canadian army seized them. It is now used as a summer resort for officers on the Great Lakes who go there and enjoy what was once an Indian reserve. The homes Indian soldiers fought for have now been lost because the Canadian government refuses to honour an
agreement that it made with the people of Stoney Point during the war.
You could lose your Indian status simply by joining the army. You could lose your status by voting, as is the right of every Canadian citizen or every citizen in a province. In many cases, by signing up to vote you lost your Indian status. Who else in this country has to lose their status and their culture by signing up and exercising their right as a Canadian citizen or the citizen of any province to vote in an election? Yet this is the kind of thing that we did and continue to do to native people.
The Indian Act and the Indian administration in this country was designed to liquidate Indians as a separate culture in Canada and to assimilate those people into the dominant society. It was futile. It was fruitless. It could not be done.
A second thing that we did to native Indians when we found out that parents have a great deal of influence on their children in matters of education and matters of culture is that we decided to set up Indian residential schools. We would take those children away from the influence of their parents and their cultural influence. We would take them away from their roots and from their homes and we would put them in with other children from all over the country who, in many cases, spoke different languages, and we would educate them all together so that they would become more white than their parents were. That is how the residential school system operated. We put them under the control of religious communities that saw Indian religions and cultural beliefs as satanically inspired. In many of those schools, the children were brutalized. The revelations that have come out of Mount Cashel and other institutions recently would pale in comparison to some of the things that happened in Indian residential schools over the last 100 years.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know if you saw the film on CBC Where the Spirit Lives. I thought it was an excellent film, and based on the stories that I have heard from my native constituents and from natives across the country, it treated very lightly the kind of brutality both against culture and against individuals that took place in those schools. If we ever want to do an investigation of the residential school system, it would produce some stories that no Canadian would be proud of.
May 1, 1990

One of the things that happened out of the residential school system and one of the things that is being debated in Manitoba today where the member comes from, is the process whereby child welfare agencies in the province were permitted to seize Indian children from their parents, take those Indian children out of their families and to adopt them into white families, or non-Indian families, or even to adopt them into the United States and to other countries around the world.
The member for Winnipeg North Centre will know the story of the native women who was recently brought back from Holland by the native organizations in Manitoba. She had been adopted into a European family in The Netherlands. They had sexually and physically abused her. They had allowed her to be a prostitute on the streets of Amsterdam. When she got cancer, they brought her back home. Her people found her and brought her back home to die. There are thousands of children in Manitoba and in all the other provinces who have experienced that same adoption and have been taken out of their homes.
There are many ways in which this country treats its Indian people unjustly. As I said, not simply when they come into contact with the justice system, but this injustice is institutionalized in the way we deal with native people.
Look at what is happening in resource conflicts around the country, Mr. Speaker. Whether it is in the Innu lands in Labrador, or any province or any region of any province, you will find the same kind of thing happening. Essentially, when governments of provinces and the federal government look at native lands or lands claimed by native people, they consider those lands as empty or as lands populated by non-persons. That allows the government to contract with foreign governments to allow the low-level flying in the Innu areas of Labrador. They consider and treat the Innu people as essentially non-persons, and Innu lands as empty lands for the purpose of resource development.
The same thing is happening in James Bay with the expansion of the James Bay hydroelectric projects. The lands of the James Bay Cree are considered empty lands, populated by non-persons. Therefore, it is possible to expand hydro reservoirs, pouring mercury into those
Supply
reservoirs which destroys the fisheries that are enjoyed by the James Bay Cree, the Inuit and Naskapi people in that area. It destroys their lands and their livelihoods and does not take their concerns into consideration at all.
I want to express some appreciation to the Government of Ontario for the recent settlement with the Temagami Anishinaabee in northern Ontario where they allowed the Anishinaabee the right to have a veto over timber allocations in certain areas that are of extreme importance to those people, and also to allow them a veto over the right to determine whether or not those trees would be cut. This is the kind of agreement and the kind of consultation process we should be looking for.
Yet the Government of Quebec, in the Barriere Lake wilderness area has refused to allow the Barriere Lake Algonquins to play a similar role in how timber is going to be allocated in that area and how resources are going to be protected, resources those native people need for their sustenance and livelihood. As a result, the Barriere Lake Algonquin people have had to take the Government of Quebec to court. The James Bay Cree are taking the Government of Quebec to court and the Innu people of Labrador are taking the Government of Canada to court. Why should this process go to court? Why should Canada not recognize its native people as important, as belonging to the land and the land belonging to them.
We need to do three things in order to right our relationship with the native people of this country. One, we have to recognize the role they have played in the founding of this country. We have to enshrine their right to self-government in the fundamental constitutional documents of Canada. We cannot wait until everybody else has been recognized. We have to recognize those who were here first, first. That is an important thing that we would have to do in order to right the relationships that we have with native people.
Second, we have to continue the lands claims process. I appreciate what has been done by the government in the Yukon and Northwest Territories with the signing of the comprehensive agreements in that area. One of the economic benefits is that will repatriate capital back into the regions, capital that has been bled out of those regions in the last little while by actions of this government that is totally market-oriented, which seems to strengthen the communities of Toronto, Montreal and

May 1, 1990
Supply
Vancouver while bleeding resources and capital from the regions.
The tremendous advantage of land claims settlements is that it recapitalizes those regions in which the wealth of this country is located. It also puts that capital in the hands of people who have had a stake in that area for the last 13,000 years and are going to have a stake in that area, let us hope, for 13,000 years and more into the future. Recapitalizing those areas is a tremendous side advantage to the land claims issue.
Finally, the one that thing we have to do, as the member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested, is to strengthen our human rights legislation. The one problem with our human rights legislation now, whether you are talking about pay equity legislation or about the Canada Human Rights Act, is there is no teeth, there is no enforcement capability within that legislation. As a result, native people do not see the human rights legislation and the employment equity legislation as an opportunity to obtain justice in this country. In fact, in many cases they have to go to human rights authorities in the United Nations or overseas in order to obtain justice in this country.
Those are the three areas: constitutional recognition, land claims solutions, and stronger human rights legislation. If we get action on those, that will deal with the concerns brought up in this House today by the member for Winnipeg North Centre.

Mr. Speaker, there were so many things that I take exception to in the comments of the hon. gentleman that I do not know where to begin. One of the things that disappointed me most was he persistently referred to the present tense when he talked about some of the historic injustices that have been done to Canadian natives and aboriginal peoples.
For instance, his characterization of our native communities as non-persons is untrue. His statement that we have marginalized them is unfair. His comments comparing our treatment of Canada's native people to
the colonial administration in the Belgian Congo is absolutely ridiculous.
The member spent much time talking about the historic injustices done to Canadian natives, which we agree with, but he spent almost no time whatsoever on all the historic changes that have taken place in recent years. He should have done that just to be fair. When talking about individuals losing the right to vote, he could have mentioned Mr. Diefenbaker's initiatives almost 30 years ago to quite properly enfranchise all native Canadians on reserves in Canada. He could have at least mentioned that.
He could have mentioned the changes that our Prime Minister and this House have undertaken to restore the native status to women who lost that through marriage. I did not hear that. I only heard one sentence toward the end of his 25-minute speech concerning the historic native land claim settlements that have been made. The whole world is looking on those. The member should be giving credit to the present Solicitor General and the new Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and congratulating them by saying: "You have put to rest to a large extent in Canada's northern territories these historic injustices that have been done". But there was only one line on that and then he immediately got into the usual NDP propaganda and condemnation of the free enterprise system. He immediately got into NDP dogma. TTie hon. member should have spent time on that.
I take exception not only to that, but to his characterization of the brutalization of native children. I will check the "blues" to see exactly what he had to say about Mount Cashel and the difficulties at the Mount Cashel orphanage. That is absolutely ridiculous. A characterization like that does not take into consideration the thousands of very dedicated men and women who sincerely tried to help native Canadians through education, who were not inspired to condemning their beliefs as being satanic, and who were not there to try and inculcate white or European values into them.
As the member was speaking, I thought of my own grand-aunt who spent almost 30 years teaching on a reserve outside of Baddeck, Nova Scotia. She was a very dedicated, responsible individual who was trying to help native Canadians, as many of us are today, and as many people from generations past in Canadian history have tried to help. But his generalizations would lead us to

believe that what was taking place was just a complete brutalization of native children and I think that was quite unfair.

speechtext: There was not much of a question. There was a comment, but I will let the hon. member rebut.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly noted a question there. I do not know if the member is denying the history of how this country has treated its native Indian people. On the issue of status, I would suggest that he look at the concerns that are being experienced today.
Up until a case was taken before the United Nations by Canadian native women about their loss of status, Canada essentially argued that they were not going to change the status issue until they changed the Indian Act. They argued that there was a process of consultation going on to change the Indian Act. That process has now collapsed. It collapsed a long time ago.
As a result, the House of Commons passed Bill C-31, over the objections of many native groups that wanted to see a more comprehensive change take place. As a result, some very serious problems have been created on many reserves across Canada. The Minister of State indicated that while the Indian Affairs budget has gone up by 8 per cent, the population of native people in this country is increasing at a far greater rate than virtually every other segment of the population. Therefore, the amount of money going to native Indians on a per capita basis is decreasing.
Sometimes the changes in status that are brought about in this House, without adequate consultation with the native people, have resulted in even more serious problems. What is going to happen on reserves when those people with their newly restored status ask for housing, for the right to education, or for the right to social services on reserves? Canada is not expanding the reserves as much as those reserves are requesting. We have created some serious problems as a result of our efforts to unilaterally reverse the position on status and assign it to what it was before. There has to be a much broader process of consultation.

I do not criticize everyone who has been involved in Indian education over the past years, nor the relatives of my questioner. In fact, many of those people contributed to the changes that took place and to doing away with the residential school system.
I have to point out to the member that when the people of Shuswap in British Columbia took a look at why their teenagers were committing suicide at such a high rate relative to the balance of the population, they took a look at what residential schools had done to the understanding of native families. By taking children away from their families, it destroyed the understanding of what the relationships were between father and son and father and daughter. It affected the understanding of the incest taboo and incest relationships.
It created family and social disintegration, and we are paying the price for that today. Even though the residential schools have been closed down, we are paying the price for those residential schools today and I think that it is worthwhile for us to take a look at exactly what price the native people are paying for that social experiment.

speechtext:
I would like to begin by repeating that the government is committed to the principle that all Canadians, without qualification, enjoy the protection of law and the right of fair treatment in all their dealings with the judicial system. Recognizing that these benefits are obtained and maintained only by virtue of the continuing efforts of all the individuals and institutions that comprise the Canadian system of justice and justice administration, the government has and will continue to work to see that that principle is upheld.
The Minister of Justice, under the authority of the Department of Justice Act, has the responsibility for "the superintendence of all matters connected with the administration of justice in Canada, not within the jurisdiction of the governments of the provinces". This mandate extends to criminal matters generally and, as the federal government has constitutional responsibility for "Indians and lands reserved for the Indians", the department, therefore, has a special interest in addressing the justice aspirations and needs of aboriginal peoples.
While many creative and innovative strategies have evolved over the course of time to address aboriginal justice problems, there remains a great deal to accomplish. The federal and provincial ministers responsible for justice have undertaken discussions with a view to better understanding the actions that will be required by each level of government in moving toward the resolution of the aboriginal justice concerns.
The Government of Canada is committed to developing a new relationship with aboriginal peoples. Since 1984, we have responded to aboriginal aspirations with a number of initiatives to increase self-reliance and autonomy. One of the most important, and one that I mentioned just recently, is the settlement of land claims and, of course, the subject of self-government.
The Prime Minister reaffirmed the government's commitment to resume discussions on aboriginal questions at a First Ministers Conference, as soon as there appears to be reasonable prospects for success. Indeed, he has
expressed the view that Canada will not be complete until this outstanding historical question is resolved.
After the patriation of the Constitution in 1982, a series of First Ministers Conferences on aboriginal constitutional questions were held, in the words of the Prime Minister, "to make self-government a practical reality for Canada's aboriginal peoples". He envisioned, "a future in which aboriginal peoples assume even greater control over matters which directly affect them". He said as well that, "all Canadians have come to revere equality as fundamental to their birthright. The aboriginal peoples of Canada are entitled to no less". That commitment is ongoing and firm.
In the context of community negotiations with selfgovernment on Indian reserves, negotiations that have been undertaken despite outstanding Constitutional discussions, the administration of justice has been identified as a matter that is open to discussion as one element of aboriginal self-government agreements.
While pursuing the means to meet the aspirations of aboriginal communities, it must, of course, be recognized that native men and women often face particular difficulties in their dealings with the justice system, whether the difficulties are described in terms of denial of justice, over-representation in our correctional facilities, discrimination, or in some other way. The reality of these problems has been drawn to the national attention in recent times, notably as a consequence of public inquiries. These concerns will continue to be brought to the national attention as the reports of the inquiries are released and the outcomes of the special consultations are made public.
There are now three judicial inquiries pertaining to aboriginal justice that have been undertaken in response to the treatment of individuals or more general conditions: The Alberta public enquiry into policing on the Blood Reserve; the recently completed Nova Scotia Royal Commission on the Donald Marshall prosecution; and the Manitoba Public Inquiry into the administration of justice and aboriginal peoples. There have been ongoing investigations supported in other provinces.
In responding to the concerns of aboriginal peoples and to the aspirations of aboriginal communities, the federal government has established a variety of programs. These programs have been developed in recognition of the special status of Indians and the particular
May 1, 1990

needs of aboriginal peoples. The Department of Justice has programs, for instance, that seek to enhance the accessibility of the justice system to aboriginal people and to facilitate greater participation in the legal profession.
In northern Canada and other areas, federal legal aid funding has supported special efforts undertaken to respond to particular legal aid needs of aboriginal people and to involve communities more directly in the management of those services. Specially designed programs of this kind are important in ensuring the generally available services respond to the particular needs of communities whose circumstances are different than those generally found in Canada.
While access to legal services is crucial to ensuring that the rights of individuals and groups are fully recognized, other kinds of activities are important. The Department of Justice, for example, supports two such programs, native court workers and public legal education.
More must be done. I could talk more about initiatives that the Department of Justice and this government are involved with. They are all aimed at ensuring that our aboriginal people receive the kind of equal and fair treatment within the criminal justice system that they and all other Canadians deserve.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest as the parliamentary secretary reviewed the government's actions. I also listened earlier to his outburst at my colleague from the NDP. He said that perhaps we were too hard and did not put this into a historical context.
One of the concerns that we have on this side is that there is a lot of historic inertia in Canada. We turn to this government and ask what it is doing. I listened carefully when the parliamentary secretary read through his notes, and I did not hear what it was doing.
One of the problems in dealing with aboriginal issues is the reality that every day another incident happens and the government remains silent. Today, during the debate, I had a phone call from my constituency office about an aboriginal woman who was mistreated in the
Supply
largest health facility in Manitoba. The stories repeat day after day.
Does the parliamentary secretary not think that the government has some obligation to recognize this problem, to deal with it honestly and to begin to take more of a promotional position rather than a defensive one in dealing with our aboriginal peoples?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada is not taking a defensive position with respect to this. I wish I had had slightly more time. I might not have been as generous to the member for Verdun-Saint Paul had I known that I would not be able to elaborate on the different areas with which the Department of Justice and this government have been involved.
The member should be aware of the native court workers program. This is a program funded by the federal government in which we attempt to involve people who are familiar with the criminal justice system with people who have come into conflict with the law. We want them to feel comfortable. There are cultural differences. There are differences of interpretation. Sometimes the language of the court can be a problem. That particular program is one that I think is very helpful and positive.
As well, with regard to public legal information, there is no question that Canadian natives are over represented in our correctional facilities. One of the things that we are trying to do, as much as possible, not just within the territories but within the provinces across the country as a whole, is to get legal information into the hands of individuals so that they have a better understanding of the criminal justice system.
As well the hon. member should be aware of the legal aid program. It is a fundamental part of our concept of justice in this country that an individual be entitled to legal representation. No one involved in the criminal justice system in this country would be unaware of the fact that very often those who come into conflict with the law are often those who do not have the means to hire a lawyer. Therefore, we help fund legal aid programs in all provinces and in the territories as well. This is a positive and important component of ensuring that native Canadians, and other Canadians as well, receive fair treatment before the courts.

We as well, of course, are monitoring very carefully the judicial and public inquiries that I alluded to briefly. We are very concerned about those. When those inquiries identify areas in which the federal government can be helpful, of course we will look at those very carefully with a view to taking positive actions in this area.
