Mr. Speaker, I will, by utilizing the means of a point of order as well, confirm to the House that I was informed of this approximately half an hour ago. As soon as I was told of the sad and tragic incident I immediately proceeded to inform the minister so that he could verify those facts prior to rising in the House to state that in fact Mr. Matthew Pyke, who I understand is a 20-year-old man, was killed. I believe that he died as a result of gunshot wounds received on the Mohawk community of Akwe-sasne.
This is a sad event which goes to show how urgent are the actions of our government, the government of the United States and all parties involved in finding a settlement to this most tragic issue unfolding right here, less than 50 miles from Parliament Hill.
I am going to take another moment or two and I beg your indulgence, Mr. Speaker. It does not seem possible that less than an hour's drive from here people are shooting at each other with machine guns, tossing hand grenades and so on. When we watch on television events such as that going on in lands far away, in Lebanon or elsewhere, we find it difficult to conceive. To think that it
is happening right here on our doorstep is nothing short of mind-boggling.
I extend to the family of Mr. Pyke and his friends and relatives, and to the Mohawk community of Akwesasne, my condolences and those of my colleagues.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the subject before the House today. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Walker) has proposed a topic for debate which seems very appropriate in the present circumstances.
The relationship of aboriginal peoples with our justice system has been the focus of attention for a number of years. Recent studies have shown that all things being equal, aboriginal people are more likely to come into contact with the criminal justice system than the rest of the population.
Under our federal system, justice is an area of shared jurisdiction and its complexities are not always easy to grasp. In addition, the system is largely based on a culture and values that are foreign to the traditional aboriginal culture and values. It operates in an environment that is equally foreign, in languages that are not their own.
We have all at some time or other heard alarming statistics on the involvement of aboriginal people in the criminal justice system. I will not give any figures today. I merely wish to point out that the causes of the problem are complex and deep-seated, and that the justice system alone cannot be held responsible nor can it be expected to provide all the answers. However, some definite improvements are readed to make the system more receptive to the problems and aspirations of our aboriginal fellow citizens. Public inquiries in Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Alberta are examining the way the system treats aboriginal people. The government is taking the requisite steps to improve the way aboriginal people are treated by the system, and it intends to co-operate with them and do everything in its power to enable them to take their rightful place in Canadian society.
The government is aware that the legislation, the programs and the staff that implement them must reflect a better knowledge and understanding of aboriginal people, their customs and their way of life; that it is important that our Canadian laws be understood and observed by all Canadians; and that some of our laws are
May 1, 1990

simply obsolete. It has undertaken a thorough review of federal legislation, and in recent years, a number of bills have been passed in this House to correct this problem.
This process is far from over, and the task that awaits us, as members of this House, is an impressive one. However, legislation alone is not enough. It must be understood and effectively enforced. Our justice system, the way it treats individuals and access to justice itself must be fair, open and dynamic.
To achieve these objectives, the government has decided to examine the needs, concerns and demands of aboriginal people. There have been consultations in various areas. For instance, a recent study looked at aboriginal people in the correctional system. It found that problems caused by the number of aboriginal people in the prison environment are aggravated by the fact that these individuals do not form an homogeneous group and that their needs and characteristics vary, depending on the cultural groups to which they belong and according to their rural or urban origins.
The consultations that took place during the study reflected a lack of understanding on the part of the justice system of aboriginal peoples and their cultures. One of the study's recommendations was to expand the use of elders as consultants in federal penitentiaries. It was found that the role of elders had increased spectacularly during the past ten years and that many of the people consulted were convinced that their involvement could be even more important at a crucial stage in the correctional process. It was recognized that the elder's point of view could provide insights into certain cases and thus simplify decision-making by the National Parole Board. It was also found that recruitement of native workers by the system would help establish better commmunications, since increasing the number of native workers would improve the system's general understanding of and sensitivity to the needs of native inmates.
Another study, this time on policing in the reserves, was ordered to ensure that reserves would have access to appropriate police services, commensured are level and quality with those provided in other communities in the
Supply
same region. However, the study found that one could not expect the same results in communities where the circumstances were different. Services had to be adapted to the local culture and local needs.
The task force, however, recognized the fact that the federal government was under pressure to expand all major programs for Indians. They must realize that the federal government is less able to do so, for financial reasons, although the budgets have increased considerably in constant dollars in recent years, and that various federal policies to give Indian communities some real control have been developed, especially the policy of negotiating self-government with Indian groups.
Consultations are now in progress on the conclusions and recommendations of this study. The Canadian government favours native self-government and their increased participation in police services. The study concludes that for this purpose, and to better meet the aspirations and special needs of bands, steps should be taken so that Indians can begin to participate more in the major decisions on policing the reserves.
These findings apply to all aspects of the justice system. It is important for us to be as aware as possible of the needs, concerns and requirements of native people and of the obstacles we face. We must listen carefully to our native fellow citizens and understand them. We must work to ensure their representation in all institutions of the justice system at all levels. We must create institutions that can meet their needs.
Some programs are already in place to meet some of the identified needs. Consultations are going on with the native people to improve existing programs and to develop and implement new ones.
I said earlier that drafting legislation is not all; the law must also be understood. The Native Courtworker Program is probably the best-known federal native justice initiative. The services of native courtworkers to help accused natives understand and obtain legal and social services are available to any native charged with violating a federal or provincial law or municipal bylaw, including any young person within the meaning of the Young Offenders Act who is accused or suspected of breaking a federal or provincial law or a municipal bylaw. Eight

May 1, 1990
Supply
provinces and territories participate with the federal government in this initiative.
Another program to make it easier to understand the system and the law and to promote access to justice is the funding, together with the provincial and territorial governments, of organizations that provide legal information services to Canadians. These agencies, located in every jurisdiction, can provide the target public with publications and documentation adapted to different communities in the language and at the level of understanding of the intended audience. Some programs offer evening courses for adults or open-line shows on the system and current legislation. For example, the Community Legal Education of Manitoba received financial assistance this year from the Canadian government for the "Feeling Yes, Feeling No" Project, which is intended to make native communities aware of sexual abuse of children and family violence. The purpose of this project is to help residents of rural areas, especially native people and their children, better understand the main points and the principles underlying amendments to the Criminal Code dealing with child sexual abuse.
What I have said so far only skims the surface. The government is determined to play a positive leading role in improving our justice system. In co-operation with the provincial and territorial governments, native leaders and communities and non-governmental organizations, the government has done a lot to identify our roles. The problems are manifold and complex, but there are also many signs that the will to deal with these issues exists more than ever before and that dialogue is open with all concerned. Everyone has shown a desire to take part in it.
The government is determined to continue dealing with these issues and to make major improvements in the field of justice for native people. This is a priority.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that this is not the best time for me to be making a speech. I am sure the whole House would understand why, given the incident I was made aware of not that many moments ago.
Perhaps I should commence my remarks by wishing, praying, that there will be no more loss of life. I say this message not only to the members of this House but to anyone in and around Akwesasne who may be listening to this debate. I pray that cooler heads will prevail and that each and every one will understand that the violence has to come to an end. Needless to say, any further violence will not enhance that prospect.
Having said that, I would like to take a few moments to talk about the community of Akwesasne, to describe it a bit for some of our colleagues so that we can all understand what we are talking about. Perhaps that will assist us as well in understanding why we have some of the problems we have there now.
The Mohawk government paper on aboriginal rights and the Canadian Constitution, prepared for the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs in October 1985, described the community of Akwesasne in the following way:
It is an understatement to say that Akwesasne is "unique". -We are the only community in North America to straddle two countries, two provinces and one state. Within Akwesasne there are three forms of government consisting of the Tribal Council, the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne and the Traditional Council. Each are very distinctive and serve to form a very dynamic and non-apathetic government system. The leadership of Akwesasne are faced with problems no other similar entity would dream of because of the geographic and jurisdictional boundaries of our community. The government of particularly the Canadian portion of the reserve is complicated by the jurisdictional horrors of inter-provincial politics and federal responsibility. The argument is always whether a question should be deferred to the province of Quebec or Ontario or to the federal government in Canada. Bureaucratic red tape and an antiquated Indian Act serve to inhibit change in the relations between the leaders of Akwesasne and the government of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, that short passage expresses to us some of the difficulties, some of the jurisdictional problems, of the Mohawk community of Akwesasne. Picture yourself for a moment, Mr. Speaker, as a resident of the village of St. Regis. Perhaps your brother or sister lives on another part of the same reserve, call it another part of the same town to use language that you and I are familiar with, and we call that part of town Cornwall Island.
You both get up at nine o'clock in the morning and decide that you are going to go over to the U.S. side of the reserve. A resident of St. Regis just walks across. It takes approximately 30 seconds. As a matter of fact, you
May 1, 1990

may not even realize you are crossing the boundary between the two countries because some of those concrete monuments are missing and weeds and grass are growing around those that remain so you are not too sure where they are. There are no customs agents, immigration officials or anything like that.
Your brother or sister, whom I have fictitiously described, who lives in the other part of the same town, to use our language again, on Cornwall Island, crosses over to the U.S. side of the same reserve. Of course, he or she has to go through customs, is stopped there and perhaps searched, which is quite normal when you are dealing with boundaries. They can then go on their merry way to the American side of the reserve.
Think about it the following way, Mr. Speaker. If you are a resident of Cornwall Island and you want to visit your relative in the village of St. Regis, both of which are on the Canadian side, you have to go through U.S. customs to get to the United States because that is the only way of getting back into Canada on the other portion of the reserve.
One cannot help but scratch his head and ask why these laws are so crazy. I guess you just shrug your shoulders and say: "White man's rule, they do not really make much sense", and you continue doing what you are doing.
If it were that easy, Mr. Speaker, if you could just shrug your shoulders and go on your merry way, perhaps it would all be simple. But that is an example of the frustration people have with a set of rules which are applied totally arbitrarily because, of course, in two communities on the Canadian side on the same reserve they are not applied the same way.
Let us imagine ourselves in the shoes of a person like Grand Chief Mike Mitchell, who is an elected person, like you and I are, Mr. Speaker, doing his best to govern the Canadian side of the reserve. Grand Chief Mike Mitchell or his U.S. counterpart have no choice of whether they are the chief of one side or the other rather than the whole entity. The structure is that way. There is this artificial boundary right down the middle of the village. There is nothing they can do about it.
Supply
So there are two jurisdictions at the native level plus, of course, the historic traditions that fall in there as well. Of course, Mr. Mitchell is certainly not a perfect human being. Neither am I, Mr. Speaker, neither are most of us here, but he is there and elected, trying to govern as best he knows how the community of Akwesasne.
For the purpose of this discussion let us imagine there is an argument between an individual and the local police on the Canadian side. What do you do? You have to cross from St. Regis where the police force is to Cornwall Island where this problem is occurring. Of course, in order to do that you have to get the police cruiser on to the American side.
As you know, you cannot bring a gun into the United States legally. So you leave your gun in the police station since you cannot bring it in the car because your car has to go on the American side in order to come back to Canada to administer the police work.
Once you get back into Canada on Cornwall Island you are a policeman without a gun. That is fine if the other person does not have a gun either, I suppose, but what if he or she does? Then you are not equipped to handle the situation.
The same occurs, of course, if the residents of Snye on the Quebec portion of the reserve need services offered by the police force. The same potential situation occurs in the area of ambulances and all kinds of other services because of artificial boundaries placed there by our ancestors which fall right in the middle of that community-
The ancestors of the proud residents of Akwesasne have been living there for a very, very long time and it is a shame that we are unable to provide the mechanisms necessary to at least make Akwesasne a little bit easier to govern. Even if we are able to make the place a little bit easier to govern, that perhaps would not solve all the problems that we have there now.
In addition to the inter-jurisdictional difficulties that I have described, we also have to deal with those people who seize such opportunities as they see fit to establish places that they deem are appropriate to serve their own interests. I refer here to the establishment of casinos,

May 1, 1990
bingo halls and so on. I understand that there are approximately half a dozen of them.
It should be remembered by us all that at Akwesasne all of those facilities, at least all the ones that I know of, are located on the U.S. side of the reserve. In a strange coincidence the U.S. side of the reserve has no police force at the present time. It was disbanded some time ago. My colleague from Stormont-Dundas is sitting beside me here. He lives only a few miles from Akwesasne and he will know, of course, that the American side of the reserve has no such thing, as we speak today, as a police force. There is no one on the American side who administers any kind of policing, save and except perhaps the so-called warrior society which has decided on its own that this is what it should be doing. On the Canadian side, of course, there are the police forces that I was describing awhile ago.
So when you have that situation of one-half of the reserve with almost total anarchy, it is fertile ground for the lawlessness that I was talking about before. So it is not a coincidence that that is where the casinos, the gambling halls and bingo halls and all those other things are located. It is not a coincidence either that they have not established themselves on the Canadian side where there exists Grand Chief Mitchell, his council, and all the other things that are there.

Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to rise in the House today and ask my colleagues in the other place to pass Bill C-21 without further delay.
We have a responsibility to improve our training and labour force adjustment programs, and that is what Bill C-21 is supposed to do.
The total cost of the amendments proposed by the Liberal senators is nearly $1.7 billion annually. We don't have that kind of money!
Mr. Speaker, how long will it take the Senate to release the funds that will enable all Canadians to have access to better training and better jobs?

Now we have roughly the following situation. The residents of Akwesasne see those casinos. They see, of course-and I have to say it-the undesirable elements that sometimes seem to surround those establishments, and they decide that they want no part of this. That is understandable. I live in a small village. It is not, of course, a native village, but I would not want those casinos in my own village, which has its own unique little character.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I will draw your attention to the clock and continue immediately after Question Period.

Mr. Speaker, today, the board of directors of the federal Superannuates National Association is meeting in Ottawa to discuss pension reform. They are very concerned, so concerned in fact that today they are sending a telegram to the Prime Minister to ask him to finally bring legislation into the House to deal with this matter.
In 1986, the government introduced legislation to reform federal pensions, recognizing the need for pension reform. That legislation died when the 1988 election was called.
Since then, the President of the Treasury Board has declared on numerous occasions that he intends to introduce new superannuation reform legislation. To date, no such legislation has been introduced.
Federal superannuation funds are growing at a rate of approximately $5 billion per year. There is plenty of money for pension reform. There is plenty of need for pension reform. All that is lacking is the political will of

this federal government and a commitment to pensioners across the country.

Mr. Speaker, on Sunday evening in my riding part of the wharf at Stanley Bridge collapsed.
It collapsed because of a lack of funding from this government for wharf and harbour maintenance. Fortunately, no one was hurt.
It is the responsibility of this government to ensure that wharves and harbours do not reach life-threatening conditions.
I have toured the wharves and harbours in my riding, and I know that there are many places where poor wharf conditions demand the attention of this government. My colleagues and I have been asking for financial assistance since we were elected in 1988.
I urge the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to come to my province, to visit the harbours and witness the terrible wharf conditions fishermen must face.
This government must plan ahead and make wharf repair a priority. The fishermen of Prince Edward Island deserve safe facilities. The situation in Stanley Bridge needs immediate action.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise the House that the month of May has been designated as National Motorcycle Awareness Month by the Canada Safety Council.
The Hon. Doug Lewis, Minister of Transport, has endorsed this worthy, new safety endeavour which is aimed at reducing road accidents, injuries and deaths during the summer months.
The theme of the safety campaign "Roads are for Sharing" aims at fostering a strong, positive attitude among all road users to abide by the rules of the road.
Safety is a shared responsibility. Motorcylists must drive responsibly and follow the rules of the road. Motorists need to be extra vigilant for motorcyclists and bicyclists who are sharing the road with them.
I particularly wish to acknowledge the Canada Safety Council's efforts in educating parents of young children about the importance of bicycle helmets. We must not forget that head injuries are by far the leading cause of traffic fatalities involving cyclists.
I invite all members of this House to support this latest road safety initiative.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians realize the hypocrisy of this government and the Governor of the Bank of Canada when they insist that Canadians restrain wage increases to control inflation, while at the same time they keep interest rates high and continue to raise taxes, and while employees of the Prime Minister's office and the Bank of Canada have received wage increases estimated by some at up to 20 per cent on an annual basis.
Nepean's Margaret Knight, a 35-hour weekly volunteer co-ordinator of a food shelter, serves breakfast and lunch daily to hundreds of women and children. Due to this government's cut-backs to the Canada Assistance Plan, the agency will face severe financial restrictions. The double standards of this government are becoming ever more frustrating.
In Ontario alone, CAP, which was instituted in 1966 to provide basic necessities to those in need, will see a revenue shortfall of approximately $90 million.
Are we really seeing the demise of a caring society as we have known it?
Canadians will not continue to be fooled by these drastic measures.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise today to congratulate the winners of the first provincial competition of Skills Canada that took place April 21 in Hamilton.
Skills Canada is part of the Skills Initiative Program. Last year, Canadian students attended the competition in the United States as observers and guests. This year, 40 Ontario winners will compete with 7,000 other partici-

May 1, 1990
pants in the United States Skills Olympics to be held in Tulsa, Oklahoma in June.
It will be the first time Canada has been represented in this North American event.
The competitive categories cover a wide range of expertise. Here are a few examples: air-cooled gasoline engine repairs, architectural drafting, carpentry, woodworking, cosmetology, culinary arts, and the list goes on.
I congratulate them all on a job well done and wish them the best of luck in the upcoming event.
These are the varied sorts of skills training that stand to gain by the passage of Bill C-21.1 would encourage all members to seriously consider what is at stake by obstructing the passage of Bill C-21.

Mr. Speaker, yet another incident has called this government's low-level flying program into question. A British Tornado aircraft crashed yesterday near the Canadian Forces Base at Goose Bay. The aircraft was reportedly flying 10 to 20 miles outside the designated zone.
Why was the aircraft there?
This incident certainly casts even more doubt on the DND's claim that the Innu will not be over-flown if they simply tell the defence department where they will be.
What about safety? Tornado aircraft crash a lot in Britain, so you would think that our government would have assessed the risk of continuing to allow them to fly in Canadian airspace.
I again ask the government to stop low-level flights all together. This crash is another example of how these flights are not only a violation of Innu sovereignty and an impediment to peace, but they are also unnecessarily dangerous for people and the environment.

Mr. Speaker, languages should unite people, not divide them.
The Meech Lake Accord is more than a question of language and culture: it is the gathering together of all the people of a great and diverse country, and it means accepting others in a spirit of generosity and tolerance.
Meech Lake also means uniting the strengths of ten provinces.
Meech Lake means understanding and accepting that Quebec is the wellspring of French Canada.
No province will be diminished by accepting the facts as they are. Should Canadians turn their backs and say no to part of their daily reality?
Quebec has been distinct for a century, Mr. Speaker. Why should it no longer be distinct in 1990?
I am a francophone, the member for Beauce in Quebec, and I belong to that great Canada my parents used to describe as a generous and tolerant country.
I say to the leaders of Manitoba and Newfoundland that wisdom lies in accepting the fact that one's neighbours may be different. This fact does not prevent the economy of your province from expanding or your people from participating in this vast country of ours, where anglophones, francophones and allophones accept and respect each other.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, roughly one month ago the task force reports of the Canadian Labour Market and Productivity Centre on the government's Labour Force Development Strategy was released.
In its entirety, the study asserts that Canada requires a new attitude and approach to labour force training so that our workforce can better meet the evolving demands posed by structural demographic and technological change.
Of particular interest and importance is the task force reports on human resource planning. Both the labour and business report press the need and requirement for basic skills training in literacy and numeracy.
These skills should be promoted on a universal basis since they form the foundation upon which higher development skills and retraining can be based.
I trust that our government will heed this advice and devote additional resources to basic skills training. The funds envisaged in Bill C-21, the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, could be instrumental in this regard. I urge our friends in the Senate to play a more constructive role in our pursuit of an effective national training effort.

subtopic: TAX BENEFITS FOR NORTHERN AND ISOLATED
TAX BENEFITS FOR NORTHERN AND ISOLATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present system of tax benefits for northern
and isolated areas is unfair. Some communities qualify, while others right next door do not. There is not a single community in the riding of Restigouche-Chaleur that qualifies for these benefits. Northern Canadians and residents of isolated areas rejected the recommendations of the Task Force on Tax Benefits.

The people of my riding are entitled to this tax benefit since they have to incur the extra costs of living in an isolated area, which include travelling long distances to obtain specialized health care, post-secondary education and many other goods and services.

The federal government must introduce a new system that will give remote communities like those in Northern New Brunswick the same tax benefits that are available to residents of similar communities.

Mr. Speaker, May 1 is a day often associated with the labour movement throughout the world.
Organized workers in Canada enjoy a standard of living excelled by few of their counterparts in other countries of the world. Collective bargaining rights in Canada are among the strongest in the world, and so they should be.
Canada is a strong, democratic country currently enjoying the dynamic leadership of a Prime Minister and government with the courage and the integrity to lead, and the ability to prepare this country for the 21st century.
The labour movement has an important role to play in preparing Canada for its place in the competitive world of the next century. I encourage all labour leaders to work with our government in its effort to ensure a prosperous future for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, interest rates are continuing to rise-21 times since this government was elected.
Not since the dying days of the previous Liberal government have interest rates been so high and so harmful to Canadians.
It is time this government recognized the harm that high interest rates are doing to farmers. Commodity prices remain too low to meet the cost of production. Farm debt has escalated beyond the $22 billion mark. In Saskatchewan, 1,000 farm families each year are leaving the land.
High interest rates are contributing to increased farm bankruptcies, foreclosures and forced sales. It is time for this to stop.
Governments can control and manage the levels and effects of interest rates. Canadian farm families should expect no less from their federal government.
I call on the government today to take the necessary steps to reduce interest rates so that Canadian farmers can begin to get control of their farm finances.

Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to remind members of the House and the general public that this is Mental Health Week.
For the past 30 years the Canadian Mental Health Association has co-ordinated events to raise national public awareness aimed at reducing the stigma of mental illness and at encouraging community acceptance of those in need of mental health services.
The Department of National Health and Welfare is pleased to collaborate with the CMHA in this worthwhile event to draw attention to the importance of mental health issues.
This year's slogan for Mental Health Week is "Working Together for Mental Health". All Canadians are invited to give their full support to the Mental Health Week events that the local branches of the CMHA have planned in their communities.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is involved in five peacekeeping operations around the world, including increasing its commitment to the UN forces in Central America and may become an important participant in a possible UN operation in Cambodia.
The demands for UN peacekeeping and Canada's participation will likely increase further given the upsurge in ethnic tensions in the developed and developing world, increasing disputes over ocean sovereignty and mounting trans-border environmental dangers.
The federal government has through budget cut-backs eliminated the acquisition of new communications equipment and new light observation helicopters, both important aspects of Canadian peacekeeping.
For example, Canadian peacekeepers face situations wherein they can barely supply cold weather gear for themselves, let alone to other participants involved in cold weather peacekeeping operations.
It is not enough that the government engage in internal reviews to reassess the new demands upon Canadian defence and foreign policy. We must allow the public to have input in these reassessments and be willing to provide the necessary financial support to ensure that its present and future commitments do not ring hollow.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
Yesterday, in response to my questions about the contraction of the Canadian economy in January and February, the minister said by way of reply:
- I acknowledged in my last budget that we expected to have a slowdown in the economy this year. We expected that in the first half of this year. So there are no surprises here.
May 1, 1990

In his budget the minister also predicted that interest rates would average only 11.1 per cent this year.
I ask the minister this. How is he going to achieve this 11.1 per cent interest rate target when interest rates in Canada have already gone above the 13.8 per cent level? Is it not time for him to admit that his interest rate projections in his budget are now totally obsolete?

Mr. Speaker, I think if the Leader of the Opposition would notice the calendar he would see that we are one month into the fiscal year. We have 11 months to go before we have to review what the total impact of interest rates are.
Certainly, interest rates are high, and we are reviewing this on a regular basis. But let us not jump to conclusions too quickly before we see how things develop further.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, everybody else in this country has already reached the conclusion that interest rates should start coming down. For example, yesterday, Adam Zimmerman, President of Noranda Forests, speaking on behalf of the Business Council on National Issues, usually a strong supporter of this government's economic policy, said: "The BCNI's thinking is that high interest rates have gone too far, and it's time to bring them down."
The voice of the Business Council on National Issues has been added to the voices of major business organizations like the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Real Estate Association.
Why will the minister not listen to these major business organizations and agree that interest rates have already gone too far, that it is time to bring them down, and therefore start bringing them down today?

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to what Mr. Zimmerman and other leading commentators in the business community have to say about these matters. Their views are important, obviously. They employ a lot of people.
I think what Mr. Zimmerman is pointing out is that there is a difference between the experiences that they are having in the goods sector-the manufacturing and resource sectors of the economy, which are very clearly
Oral Questions
feeling the effects of the monetary policy that we have been following-as compared to the service sector, or other levels of government, which are not responding in the normal ways to the interest rate policy that we have been following and are keeping their prices and wage settlements up to reasonably high levels.
It is that distinction, that difference between the goods sector on the one hand and the service sector on the other hand, which makes it particularly difficult to deal with at this point in time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is only one interest rate in this country. The minister forgets we don't have a range of interest rates. We have only one, and Mr. Zimmerman and his colleagues have asked for an immediate reduction in this interest rate. Mr. Speaker, yesterday, Doug Peters, chief economist for the Toronto-Dominion Bank, commented on the policy of the Minister of Finance, saying that:
The economy was idling, that after the brakes had been applied for two consecutive months, the machine had finally stopped.
I want to ask the minister why the government maintains a policy whose purpose is to stop the economic machinery completely. Why does the Minister of Finance want to drive the Canadian economy into a deep recession?

Mr. Speaker, let me correct a couple of things that the Leader of the Opposition said.
First, this policy is not designed, to use his words, to stop the economic machinery completely.
Second, it is not designed, again to use his words, to drive the economy into a deep recession.
What I have said on many occasions in the past is that we are trying to avoid that recession by slowing down the level of activity in the economy so that we can reduce and eliminate the inflationary pressures that are there. We are seeing some signs of inflationary pressures easing, using some measurements, but in using other

May 1, 1990
Oral Questions
measurements they are not easing. That is the problem that I referred to in my second answer to him.
If we are able to take these inflationary pressures out of the economy, then we can look forward with confidence to many more years of non-inflationary sustainable growth. That is the objective of this government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance who just referred to the fact that it is early in the year and that the Leader of the Opposition in referring to the high interest rates should wait for awhile.
Why does the minister believe that Canadians should have confidence in his projections as they relate to the interest rate that he predicted would be at 11.1 per cent when last year in his budget he predicted that by the end of the year the average interest rate would be at 10 per cent? Why would he be right this year when he was so wrong last year?

Mr. Speaker, let me draw to my friend's attention the fact that the one-year deficit projection of this government in the five years that we have projected the deficit has been out an aggregate of something in the order of $2.5 billion. The previous five years under Liberal projection it was $26.5 billion. That is a factor of 10 to 1.
Hear, hear!
Surely, that should give Canadians a much better degree of confidence in our ability to project than was the case in previous years.

Mr. Speaker, my question for the Minister of Finance is quite simple. What we want to know is based on the projections in his Budget. Does he still maintain that his projections on the deficit, which was supposed to be $28 billion, will be borne out, and will the average interest rate for the current year still be 11.1 per cent? Does he maintain his position, as stated in the Budget, with respect to interest rates and the Canadian deficit?

Mr. Speaker, what I was pointing out in my first response to
my hon. friend is that we on this side of the House do manage to keep to our projections. We have worked hard to manage through our projections in each year.
Hear, hear!
How about your promises?

I hear some catcalls from the other side. I do not think that those catcallers heard that the total deviation from our budget deficit projections is $2.5 billion-one-tenth the deviation under the Liberals in the previous five years.
I pointed out that we are one month into the fiscal year. There are things that will put upward pressure on the deficit, and that is what higher interest rates will do. But, also, the higher level of inflation increases revenues. So it is not all one way.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Solicitor General.
As he will know, a 22-year old Mohawk resident of the Akwesasne reserve was fatally shot today, following what was described as a nine-hour gun battle. This is a situation which has been developing for many months, even many years.
My question to the Solicitor General is this. Will the RCMP now intervene? What steps will the government take to deal with this tragic situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ministers of the government and all members of this House are indeed saddened to learn of the tragic escalation of violence which occurred overnight at the Akwesasne Mohawk Reserve.
We extend our sympathies and those of all Canadians to the families and friends of the young Mohawk man who has lost his life as a result of the senseless violence that continues at Akwesasne.
I am informed that a week ago, the three councils from the reserve came to the federal government-in fact, they met with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development-and specifically asked for the RCMP to intervene, to bring law and order to the reserve.

May 1, 1990

Earlier this morning we were informed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who learned from the Surete du Quebec, that 22-year old Matthew Pyke died at 10.57 a.m. in hospital in New York State of gunshot wounds. Mr. Pyke, a resident of Hogansburg, New York, was shot at Snye, Quebec.
My colleagues and I are dismayed that the situation has deteriorated to this point. One death is one death too many. We have and will continue to strive to find a peaceful solution to this very serious and difficult problem.
As the hon. member and other members know, we were visited by the elected leadership, the traditional leadership, of the Mohawk communities last Wednesday, not a month ago as the member indicates, and have sought working with officials of various federal departments, officials of the two provincial governments of Ontario and Quebec, the State of New York and the United States government, to find a peaceful solution to this problem. Those efforts are continuing at an escalated pace today.

Mr. Speaker, in no way do I mean to diminish my respect for the government's concern for the death in this case. I must say that it is simply not enough to hear that the government is continuing discussions.
I ask the Solicitor General who is responsible for the RCMP if will he accede to the request that was made a week ago, as the minister has just confirmed in the House, that the RCMP move on to the reserve and establish law and order so that Canadian citizens on the reserve can be protected?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
As the hon. member would know, policing in Canada is firstly a matter of provincial jurisdiction.
Contacts were made with the Attorney General for Ontario and Solicitors General last week. They have taken actions to effect the patrols and disarmament, where possible, of those carrying arms on the Canadian side.
The member knows that the problem arises from a pro-gambling faction based in New York state.
Oral Questions
Any activity to intervene from outside the Mohawk nation requires the full consent and co-operation of several law enforcement agencies, the state and the provincial governments, as well as the two national governments.
That kind of co-ordinated approach is being discussed at the highest level, with a view to seeking a peaceful solution to this very, very serious situation.

It should be evident that the time for a peaceful solution has tragically passed.
First, the Minister of Indian Affairs has not indicated whether he ever spoke to the Solicitor General about this. My question again is to the Solicitor General.
Did he receive the request from the native groups involved?
Very particularly, did the Solicitor General, on behalf of the RCMP, seek the authority from the Ontario Provincial Police, the Quebec Police and the Americans to come on to that reserve?
He had the authority of the native people involved and of the leadership on that reserve. Did he seek the authority a week ago, before this tragedy happened?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre H. Cadieux (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been indicated by my colleague, we have here a situation that involves various jurisdictions, beginning with American and Canadian, and provincial jurisdictions with respect to where the reserve is situated on the Canadian side.
With that comes policing jurisdiction and I can assure the House and my hon. colleague in particular that we have been co-ordinating policing efforts since the situation started and particularly since we were asked last week to intervene. There have been discussions between the Attorneys General and the Solicitors General from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec and between my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs, and myself.
It is a co-ordinated effort, and as was indicated this morning by my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott- Russell, it has to be a co-ordinated effort involving also New York state before any physical intervention can occur. We have been co-ordinating this. We will continue to do so. We will act according to the circumstances.

May 1, 1990
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could preamble my question by expressing on behalf of my colleagues and I, our sympathy and regret to the family of Mr. Matthew Pyke who so tragically passed away in this most unfortunate event, which hopefully will end very soon, namely the violence at Akwesasne.
My question is for the Solicitor General. I agree with him that the approaches that have to be taken in order to have a physical intervention at Akwesasne have to be taken together on both sides of the international border. Otherwise, let's face it, nothing at all is going to happen because the arms will simply move from one side of the border to the other.
Can he report to us now what progress has been achieved this morning in the meeting he and presumably others in his department have had with the Americans in regard to restoring law and order at Akwesasne, more particularly to disarm the community of Akwesasne?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has indicated there has been a continuing co-ordination of police forces in this matter. Yesterday morning five police forces, including the state, two provincial, and the national police forces, met and agreed that a co-ordinated effort is required to deal effectively with the violence in the Akwesasne community.
As well, the Secretary of State for External Affairs wrote to Mr. James Baker last Friday and there has been high level interventions at the state department. I understand that Canada's ambassador in Washington is again approaching the State Department with a strong message of concern this afternoon.
It is our desire to see the state of New York co-operate and assist in dealing with the elements on the New York state side which appear to be provoking this incident. To this point we are not satisfied that the state of New York is responding adequately.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to direct a supplementary question to the same minister. It was only yesterday that Governor Mario Cuomo of New York finally admitted that there was a problem which necessitated an outside intervention. We all know that before that he was
claiming that this was an internal matter to be settled by Mohawks. I am sure the minister will agree that that kind of action was totally inappropriate up to that point.
Can he tell us if he still believes that Governor Mario Cuomo takes the position that it is all right to have those gambling casinos on the U.S. side? I believe, and I believe the people of Akwesasne believe, that the first element to a solution is to close down those casinos, leave them closed, disarm the community and then worry about those other things afterwards.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member would agree that this is not the place to engage in a debate with Governor Cuomo, but it is in fact the case that in order to effect a peaceful solution of this serious and tragic occurrence the democratically elected leadership of the Mohawk nation in all of its parts, which represents the majority of the Mohawk people, must be respected. A way must be found through some form of diplomatic or mediated process to have the majority wishes of the Mohawk people respected.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Revenue. The staff of the Canada Customs office presently located in Cornwall are scheduled to be moved to Cornwall Island on the Akwesasne reserve on May 11.
Given the tragic event of earlier today would the minister accept my suggestion to postpone this move indefinitely?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when conflict on the island began to escalate some time ago I immediately gave instructions to my officials to postpone any movement of additional staff to Cornwall Island.
May I point out as well, as I told his colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell last Friday, that we also entered into an agreement some months ago with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Ontario Provincial Police to protect customs facilities and officers and the travelling public on Cornwall Island.
May 1, 1990

We have further improved the facility from a standpoint of additional security, including the expansion and improvement of the building. I can assure the hon. member that as far as the customs officers and the travelling public is concerned, every step has been taken to protect them from any potential danger.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is to the same minister. I wonder if he would commit today, to the House, a full review of the appropriateness moving any officials to the new location on Cornwall Island?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just confirmed to this House that I have put a stop to any potential move of additional personnel to Cornwall Island until the situation on the island stabilizes.
The request at the beginning, prior to any concerns affecting anyone on the island, was to try to utilize expanded facilities and provide a greater service for the travelling public. While these conflicts continue to take place or even potentially exist on Cornwall Island, no movement of additional personnel is going to take place.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. The Canadian economy at this stage is already suffering serious problems. Yet yesterday, our ambassador to the United States made a public speech to U.S. businessmen and others, talking about threats to our unity and internal division here in Canada. This sort of alarmist talk in Washington hurts us economically.
Could he tell the House if this speech by Mr. Burney was fully discussed with the government and if not, why it was not discussed.

Mr. Speaker, the speech by Ambassador Burney, what appeared to include a question and answer session, appeared to deal with some questions that had been raised in Washington a few days ago by Mr. Jacques Parizeau, the leader of the Parti Quebecois, who visited Washington and who proceeded to deliver himself of some views about how casual and how harmless the breakup of Canada might be.
Oral Questions
Ambassador Burney proceeded yesterday to disabuse Americans and I hope, a few Canadians, of those notions and indicated that indeed if there were serious consequences in Canada they would manifest themselves in most unattractive and unhelpful ways. Ambassador Burney made a very strong and I thought persuasive statement in favour of the strength and the unity of this nation and that is what he is in Washington to do.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
I have here not elements from a question and answer session, but notes for an address from Mr. Burney sent from the Embassy in the United States. We are not talking about something casual and off the top of his head.
I want to ask the Prime Minister if we are, as a country, simply some sort of banana republic that is supposed to talk about our constitutional issues in Washington.

Does the Prime Minister think it makes good sense to wash our dirty linen in Washington? Does that make sense, according to the Prime Minister?

Mr. Speaker, I had no idea Ambassador Burney's speech would offend the sensibilities of the hon. member. President Bush was here a few weeks ago, and when asked what he thought of the debate on the Meech Lake Accord, he said he did not want to intervene in a domestic debate. However, if you want to know my opinion and that of my government, we are in favour of a united and prosperous Canada. That has been the strength of this nation for 125 years. I hope the hon. member has no objection to that.
I did not see the text of the Canadian ambassador's speech before he made it, but I trust him. He is old enough to know how to behave, and he is doing a very effective job in Washington. If, either in answer to a question or directly, he touched on any matter concerning the strength and unity of this nation, he was right to do so. Does the hon. member believe that when faced with this kind of situation, our ambassador should be less than forthright and tell the Americans that nothing is happening in Canada and, in any case, it is none of their business? Citizens of a the country with whom we trade goods for a total of $200 billion annually, as neighbours and allies have every right to put questions to our

May 1, 1990
Oral Questions
ambassador. We send an ambassador to Washington to answer all legitimate questions, not to become evasive when the going gets rough.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the acting minister for employment.
Yesterday, the Valmet-Dominion Company announced the lay-off of 200 industrial workers at its plant in Montreal, and on the weekend, Pascals Hardware announced the lay-off another 180 workers in that city. This makes a total of over 9,000 lay-offs announced in Montreal during the past year, including VIA Rail, Vickers, Simpsons, General Electric, Gillette, Marconi, Cattelli and many others.
When is the government going to take the situation seriously and put forward a comprehensive program to re-establish the economy and employment in Montreal? When are we going to get some action and less words?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are aware that workers in Montreal and elsewhere in Canada are going through difficult times. That is why, as a responsible government, last April we tabled a labour force strategy with a policy for unemployment insurance reform, as a tool for this government to develop new policies and enhance our ability to compete in a globalized market. We say that this reform will help workers make up losses they would otherwise have incurred.

Mr. Speaker, we have had nothing but band-aid solutions by the government.
In a report published last month, in April, by the regroupement des departements de sante communautaire du Montreal, it was stated that one out of four Montrealers
now live in poverty. In 23 neighbourhoods of Montreal, the unemployment rate is over 15 per cent.
The fact that some of these people are working does not address the problem, because there are too many low paying, part time jobs and a lot of working poor. When is the government going to do something about this serious situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace is not telling the whole truth. He is telling his version.
The federal government has done a lot in the Montreal area. For example, he should consider the investments, particularly in the eastern part of Montreal, which he no longer talks about since the government has taken some worthwhile initiatives.
Mr. Speaker, everyone knows that the federal government has done its job. General Motors confirmed just last week that it was awarding the F series of cars, the Firebirds, to Montreal.
I personally went to Cameo in eastern Montreal yesterday, Mr. Speaker, to confirm the maintaining of 700 jobs with the workers, who were extremely satisfied. Again, I think that when you talk about Montreal, you can give your version of the facts, but someone must tell the truth about Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Fisheries.
The lobster crisis is worsening. Quebec fishermen are refusing to go out and fishermen from the Acadian peninsula will stay in port tomorrow. At $1.25 a pound, lobster does not pay enough to cover expenses.
The minister said in Caraquet last Sunday that he would consult with the interested parties. However, the government had been warned last September by all those concerned in the lobster industry.
So my question is quite simply this: Why did the minister drag his feet so much that he is still only at the consulting stage? How come he has no solution to offer these fishermen?
May 1, 1990

Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Mr. Speaker, it is easy for a Liberal member to get up and blame everyone for the prevailing conditions in the lobster market. Two months ago, I spoke with the fisheries ministers of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, for example, and at the time, I believe there was $17 million worth of lobster from last year in stock.
Inventories, I believe, still amount to about 20 per cent of 1989 production today. This is due to market conditions.
Now, I met the lobster fishermen on Sunday and I received a proposal from them that I intend to discuss with my provincial colleagues whom I am to meet next week.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. Lobster fishermen and the whole industry are in this predicament precisely because the government has failed to protect them.
As a matter of fact, I understand that the Minister of Fisheries and the Prime Minister will meet with workers and fishermen tomorrow at Inkerman in the Acadian peninsula.
Will the minister and the Prime Minister take this opportunity to unveil a support program for that industry which the Prime Minister himself had promised to protect, something he has yet to do?
Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Fisheries and
Oceans): Sure enough, Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will be in the Acadian peninsula and we will take that opportunity to urge the people to tell the bunch of unelected senators to pass the unemployment insurance reform legislation so that we will be in a position to launch the programs which the Atlantic region needs to make sure that there are opportunities other than unemployment insurance benefits.
The hon. member never misses a chance to rise in the House on behalf of various causes, Mr. Speaker, but I am still waiting for a suggestion from the Liberal Party as to how the federal government might go about settling the issue of lobster prices on international markets.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
Five and a half months have now passed since the death of our colleague Jean-Claude Malepart. Members of all parties in this House have pointed out that Mr. Malepart was a great defender of Quebecers' interests.
The people of Laurier-Sainte-Marie have been without representation for five and a half months. My question for the Prime Minister is this: When will he give us and the people of Laurier-Sainte-Marie a precise date for the election of their representative? Is he afraid to see a Jean Chretien or a second member of the NDP get elected in Quebec?
Oh, oh!
No, Mr. Speaker, the government must follow a specific timetable in calling a by-election in Laurier-Sainte-Marie-
And in Oshawa.

-and in Oshawa. It will be interesting to see the reaction of Oshawa people because the hon. member of the NDP has asked for a by-election in a Liberal riding but forgot to mention a Socialist riding.
Hear, hear.

I wish to ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
First, I can tell you that I have not forgotten Oshawa, and I can tell you that the NDP is quite prepared in both ridings. There is no problem there.
Tell us about PCBs!

I am getting to my supplementary question. The unemployment level for the people of Laurier-Sainte-Marie is nearly 20 per cent. They have already been hit hard by free trade and they are being hit hard by the economic situation for which the federal government is responsible. If the people of Laurier- Sainte-Marie do not have a representative soon, could they at least have specific programs to help them?

May 1, 1990
Oral Questions
Ask the senators that!

Mr. Speaker, I have the feeling that very shortly I will be able to set a date for a by-election or by-elections. If you feel at ease in Oshawa- Are you ready for Oshawa?

When I hear Simon de Jong say, "It's time to go", it's time to go.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. I was most encouraged last year when the Department of Transport announced short and long-term initiatives intended to improve conditions at Pearson International Airport.
At that time we were informed that fines levied against airlines which violate flight path and flight time restrictions would be raised to $10,000. Could the minister tell the House when this important initiative will be implemented.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate my hon. friend's continued interest in Pearson International Airport. In fact, we did announce that initiative last fall. In March we took additional steps vis-a-vis departure paths and changes to take-off and climbing procedures. The amendments which my hon. friend refers to will benefit the residents of Mississauga, Brampton and Etobicoke. They are presently in the drafting stage and I would hope to have them in the House very soon.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Employment and Immigration.
Many young people in my riding make every effort to acquire the skills and training they need to get properly launched in the labour market. Everyone here will know how great a challenge that can be. Governments can and do help with this but these kids need more help. Can the
minister tell us what more the government is willing to provide?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in our jobs strategy, we have programs especially for young workers. I am thinking, for example, of co-operative programs, of occupational training programs. These help young people find and, more important, keep a job.
What we as a government want to do to improve this situation, because there is room for improvement-we presented a new labour force strategy and a reform of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Using these additional funds, we can make the progress required to ensure that young people can find work and obtain the necessary training.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade, or in his absence the acting minister. A major portion of the jobs in the town of Kinsville have been lost, 429 workers are unemployed. They are unemployed because an auto parts manufacturer has decided to use the free trade agreement and relocate operations in the U.S. and Mexico. Sheller-Globe has effectively closed the Kinsville plant, opting for $5.75 an hour labour in Indiana, and $1.50 labour in Mexico.
Does the minister continue to support this deal that is driving industries out of Canada and encouraging companies to move to the U.S. and Mexico, costing constituents in my area jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we certainly do support the trade agreement. When you look at southern Ontario, we have had a major announcement made in Windsor, for example, of an aerospace company. We have had Freightliner of St. Thomas just announce over 1,200 jobs in St. Thomas alone, and at the end of the week we are going to be at a very important announcement by Cani in Woodstock where they are opening a new line and hiring hundreds of new employees.



May 1, 1990

The free trade agreement is great for southern Ontario. I wish the hon. member knew that.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the same minister. Just to point out the facts of free trade in our area, I mention the job closing today. Wayne Bus Manufacturing Company, located in Windsor, also has announced that as of June 15, 1990, 145 workers will lose their jobs.
The company has already moved half of its production to Richmond, Indiana. The company will open a Canadian sales office in the future. Within eight years the free trade agreement will allow all of this equipment to come across duty free.
How can the minister still support this agreement that is daily costing Canadians jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can support the agreement because 264,000 jobs have been created across Canada since the agreement has been put in place.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: I want to say to my hon. friend I represent the same constituency as the premier of Ontario. I received the other day through the mail a very interesting magazine Business Week, published in the United States, with a 12-page insert from the province of Ontario in which the premier of Ontario boasts about the dynamic economy of Ontario and how the free trade agreement is assisting it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for London East, a single question.

Mr. Speaker, maybe the hon. member for London West should come back to his own community and see what is happening in London, Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. With the interest rates now hovering over 14 per cent, thousands of Canadians no longer can afford to own and buy a home. Canadians who are now renewing their mortgage will have less disposable income to spend on other necessities because of the high cost of shelter. Housing construction is now grinding to a halt, leaving
Oral Questions
thousands of construction workers without steady employment. This is one of the first industries to feel the brunt of this government's recessionary policies.
With an entire industry collapsing across the country why will the minister not admit that their interest rate policy must be changed and interest rates must be reduced now?

Mr. Speaker, for almost two years we have had the premiers of the country unanimously calling for a reduction in interest rates. At that time people were saying the housing market was going to go all to hell because of the high interest rate policy.
What has happened is that for two years we had housing starts well in excess of 200,000 every month throughout that period. So I caution the hon. member on drawing conclusions too quickly.
But I acknowledge that the housing starts in the province of Ontario have turned down. I say to my hon. friend that it is important that we do have some easing back here because of the very fast pace of activity over the course of the last five or six years. These inflationary pressures are leading to the high interest rates.
If we are able to cool the economy off somewhat now and get these inflationary pressures out of the system, we will be able to see a much healthier economy in the future and avoid the blow-up that we saw in 1981 which led to that huge recession.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Prince George- Bulkley Valley, a single question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, officials from the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre are expecting a fire season similar to last year when an area the size of New Brunswick was destroyed.
A report released in Winnipeg today stated that the problems that the department had in responding to it were the ones pointed out by the forestry minister.

May 1, 1990
Supply
Can the minister assure this House and the people of Manitoba the full support of federal agencies, including the Armed Forces, so that both governments are prepared for the fire season this year?

Mr. Speaker, I very much appreciate my hon. friend's concern in this area. Forest fires are not only recognized as a major cause of C02 emissions in the atmosphere, but annually they destroy as much fibre and timber as we are processing through our mills, a $40 billion industry.
I can give the hon. member the assurance that technical experts will be available as they have been in the past to the province of Manitoba and other provinces. We will continue with our major research effort, which has proven very effective and has had impressive results in the sense that we can now, through computer modelling, predict almost any fire in any area. Admittedly, there are costs associated with the pre-positioning of response equipment.
I cannot say that the Armed Forces will be called in to assist with that, but that is an interesting idea.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Essex-Windsor on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, there was some disagreement which arose in Question Period about whether the comments of Ambassador Burney were in a question and answer session, or part of an address. I wonder if I could have the House permission to table-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is quite out of order. 1 am sorry, but that is a matter of debate and the hon. member knows that he will have to take it up somewhere else.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to set the record straight about a point of order raised today concerning the riding of
Laurier-Sainte-Marie which is temporarily without full-time representation in Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, you would know that the House of Commons does make provision for serving the people of a riding which is unrepresented or vacant as a result of death or resignation. The arrangement is simple enough: party whips, members of the opposition parties as well as government members take over the riding after the Clerk has written to the residents of the riding. Canadians ought to know that the House of commons serves the riding of Laurier-Sainte-Marie, as it does the riding of Oshawa I suppose, but I know that the constituents of Laurier-Sainte-Marie have not been left to fend for themselves. I was there last week to meet with some of the residents, Mr. Speaker. We did respond to their letters, we tried to help those who asked for assistance, and I must say that even the ministers have been co-operative in helping the citizens of Laurier-Sainte-Marie get from the government the services they need.
I think it is unfair to suggest that the riding is unrepresented or without assistance. Quite the contrary, we are doing our best to make sure these people get the services they need. It is not an easy task, granted, but we are glad to work for them.

Mr. Speaker, I want to acknowledge that during this time service is provided by the House. I believe that my hon. friend from Chambly was saying that it was time that it has a member of Parliament in the House of Commons to represent the people of that area.
