Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to take this opportunity to offer our condolences to the family of the deceased, after what happened this morning on the Akwesasne reserve.
Mr. Speaker, to many of us, the right of aboriginal people to life, liberty and security of the person has seemed very precarious during the past few days. The situation for residents on the Akwesasne reserve is alarming and dangerous. Most Canadians cannot imagine being in that kind of situation.
Mr. Speaker, it is a difficult matter, and there is also the problem of jurisdiction, since Akwesasne straddles the borders of two provinces and two countries. As you know, talks took place throughout the weekend and continued into the small hours, to try and find a peaceful solution to this problem within the Mohawk community.
For several years, the Canadian side of the Akwesasne reserve has had its own native police services, jointly financed by the federal and provincial governments. These special officers have served the community loyally and well.
Major changes led to a law enforcement system being established by the Akwesasne community, in consultation with the federal and provincial governments.
During the past decade, Indian communities have evolved considerably. Most exercise a greater degree of autonomy, while some operate under their own forms of administrative autonomy.
Today, a steadily increasing number of residents of Indian reserves across the country would like to have their own law enforcement services.
The aspirations of aboriginal people to play a greater role in law enforcement on Indian reserves were boosted by a recent report on this question. A federal interdepartmental task force recommended that the govern-
Supply
ment should continue to support law enforcement services on Indian reserves.
This important document will help us prepare for the challenges of the 90s and represents a major step in developing a consistent federal policy.
After studying crime, incarceration, population growth and employment rates, as well as expenditures and previous policies of law enforcement agencies, the task force put forward a number of principles and findings laying the foundation for future discussions.
We must point out that in-depth consultations will be the key to finding long-term solutions in response to peace and safety concerns of Indian people. Only by meeting with the people who live there and who understand how complex the issue is can we expect to solve long-standing problems.
This consultation process has already started and involves the participation of Indian communities as well as the federal, provincial and territorial governments. These meetings will lead to the drafting of a final report making recommendations to the Cabinet later this year.
The task force report identifies a number of problems some government departments and native leaders are dealing with. One of the most important problems, as illustrated by the current situation in Akwesasne, is the need to clarify the responsibilities of the federal government and those of the provinces.
Our overlapping and sometimes incompatible roles are creating problems for native people who want greater control over their territory.
While recognizing that Indian reserves are entitled to the same quality of service as similar non-native communities, the report stresses that we share the responsibility of ensuring that law enforcement forces in reserves meet community needs.
The federal, provincial and aboriginal governments will have to cooperate and work closely together to find acceptable solutions to the present problems. The report also stressed the need to establish the cost sharing mecanisms to be used by those groups.
The Indians consider as particularly important the fact that the need for an increase in their participation in the process is recognized in the report. The consequences of self-government, service management by native people,

May 1, 1990
Supply
training and operating standards as well as the hiring of native constables are among the issues examined.
We are confident that practical solutions will be found during the course of our discusions on their concerns. We believe we will soon be able to submit new options regarding the native law enforcement services in general.
The study on the law enforcement services on the reserves is not the only ongoing study relating to the peace and the safety of our native people. The Thsk Force on the criminal justice system and its consequences on the Indians and Metis in Alberta is also doing a very important job in an area inhabited by a large Indian population. The Task Force was struck under the auspices of the Government of Alberta and the Government of Canada. The announcement of its creation was made jointly by the honorable Pierre H. Cadieux, the then Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Attorney General of Alberta, Mr. Ken Rostad, the Solicitor General of Alberta, Mr. Dick Fowler, the president of the Indian Association of Alberta, Mr. Roy Louis, and the president of the Metis Association of Alberta, Mr. Larry Desmeules. The Task Force reflects a global and positive approach to the concerns of Indian and Metis groups in the province. It will examine issues affecting natives and the criminal justice system, including the disproportionately high number of natives in Alberta correctional institutions. It will also recommend solutions to problems identified in the current criminal justice process.
The study will also deal with provincial law enforcement services, legal aid, the courts, legal practices, correctional and native counselling services.
The task force, chaired by Judge Robert Allan Cawsey of the Alberta Court of Queen's Bench, will submit its report to the federal and provincial governments by December 31, 1990.
Control over justice and law enforcement services is an important step toward self-government, which has received the obvious support of many native groups.
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that control over justice and law enforcement services in reserves is also favoured by most non-native Canadians. National polls conducted in the last two years show substantial support for a separate native justice system. This issue has clearly
been brought to the fore by the Marshall inquiry, by the inquiry on native justice in Manitoba and by increased media coverage of other incidents suggesting that the criminal justice system discriminates against natives.
A 1989 Angus Reid poll indicated that 69 per cent of the population favour a separate justice system for natives, while a survey conducted by phone the same year put the level of support at 73 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I would like to go back to the unique and frightening situation in Akwesasne. It is unique because the reserve geographic configuration is creating frustrating problems in terms of jurisdiction. Because of these problems, the crimes committed have greatly exceeded the capacities of a community police service. Such a unique situation obviously demands a unique response and we are trying to find appropriate and efficient solutions.
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians are praying for an end to the violence in Akwesasne. The process is already under way to ensure such a situation never happens again anywhere else.
We must learn from the events in Akwesasne and devote all our energies and all our support to solving justice and law enforcement problems throughout the country so that native people enjoy the same protection of life, liberty and security as all other Canadians.

I would just ask the hon. member not to write to the Minister of the Environment or to make suggestions to him, because if I understand our institutions properly, it would be better to make the chairman of this study or the Solicitor General of Canada or even the Minister of Indian Affairs aware, so that this aspect and others that you and I do not have in mind now can be considered in the light of the problem and that hopefully, adequate solutions will be found.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. On debate, the hon. member for Delta.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this very important topic this afternoon. If it were not for the Meech Lake disagreement or agreement at this time, it would be one of the major points of discussion in Canada. What we are seeing in southern Ontario, Quebec and New York State at this time is a microcosm of the types of problems that we are indeed facing and as a government must deal with.
Canada's record on human rights is very good. People come from all over the world to live in this country because of the freedoms that we enjoy and we welcome others in order that they may also enjoy it. We also need to recognize that there are problems with our aboriginal population. In the past, they have not been dealt with fairly. Things are improving slowly perhaps in some areas, but more rapidly in others. Therefore, this is a good topic for discussion and for debate this afternoon.
We have made a great deal of progress. I can remember when I was a young lad that our aboriginal people were not allowed into beer parlours and could not live in certain areas, just as many of our friends from the Orient were also limited in that area. The recent inquiries that we have seen, such as the Marshall Inquiry and the Manitoba Justice Inquiry, have demonstrated very clearly that our native population has not always been dealt with fairly.
The fact has been mentioned a couple of times today that a disproportionate number of our native people find themselves in jail for offences which, if committed perhaps by a white person, would not have been as stiff. I believe that this is an example of the poverty and the disadvantage that many of our aboriginal people do face.
As a fair government and a fair country, we need to look at these problems and assist our aboriginal people in achieving the goals and aspirations to which each Canadian aspires.
One of the keys to this whole problem is the concept of self-government to which our native population has aspired. This, of course, includes increased responsibility

May 1, 1990
Supply
for their educational, judicial, and social systems that they are working within, and the economic system which must be meshed with the rest of the economy of Canada which we all must deal with.
I believe that if this is carried out in consultation with our aboriginal leaders we will indeed see increased prosperity and increased self-reliance and independence. Already, we are seeing the emergence of strong, dynamic leaders in the aboriginal community. A few years ago this was unheard of and would never have been thought possible. Yet today we are meeting these people. Indeed, the aboriginal people should be very proud of the leaders they are electing and appointing to assist them in this very important area of self-government.
There are certain areas in which the government has been able to assist the aboriginal people in this quest for self-government. We think particularly today of the native justice system. One example where we have been able to do something is the on-reserve policing services. We have discovered, through errors that governments and others have committed in the past in trying to impose one culture on another, that many mistakes and problems have developed. Developing a proper justice system and policing system that takes into account those traditions and cultures is most vital and helpful.
The number of aboriginal people in jail has already been mentioned. Last September an Angus Reid poll revealed this concern. More than half of those polled believed that native people are not treated fairly by the courts; 70 percent of Canadians believe that native people have more difficulty getting hired for good jobs than do white Canadians; most also feel that aboriginal people deserve to be a lot better off financially than they are now. It also pointed out that Canadians are more likely to support than oppose aboriginal self-government. Over half of those surveyed agreed with the statement that the Canadian Constitution should specifically recognize the right of Indians to govern themselves on their own land without interference from white society.
These are very encouraging opinions and indicate to me a large body of goodwill among Canadian people to our native population. I only hope that it increases over the years. Canadians could not do anything else but to encourage policies and programs that would enhance that ideal and goal of self-government.
Another area in which the government is assisting aboriginal and native people to look after their own affairs is through a couple of very significant programs. One I would like to mention briefly is the Alternative Funding Arrangement or the AFA in which the government allows the individual tribal councils and bands to transfer funds from one program to another. We are all familiar with the complaint that they have made over the years that they are given money for a specific project and are unable to use it in another area where it may be of more value. This program assists those bands and councils to transfer funds without going through all of the annual budgetary changes that are necessary. This speeds up the whole process. Again, there is obviously room for improvement, but it is a step in the right direction that the Canadian government is taking.
The second program I would like to mention, again very briefly, is the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Strategy. This is designed to encourage economic development and decision-making at the local level with the recognition that the economic success rests with the aboriginal people themselves. Often we have taken a very paternalistic attitude toward our aboriginal people, that they could do nothing and it required a white man to run the show. More and more we are seeing the development of the native economic leaders themselves. This is a program that I support 100 per cent. It encourages them to move out into new areas of economic development. I think of the development in my own area of a significant tourist resort. They have some choice land and through this particular program they are discussing with the government the possibility of establishing a resort.
Another area that we should mention briefly concerns the Indian Act. So often in the past this has done nothing but impede the economic, political and social development of our aboriginal communities. Specifically, we are talking of the review of the lands and revenues, and trust review. This review is being used to examine the agreements between the various bands and councils so that they can be made more effective and utilized by our native populations for their own ends rather than having to depend on the bureaucracy in Ottawa or other major centres.

May 1, 1990

This produces an opportunity for a review in consultation with the bands and councils. This is an area which I feel could be expanded in the future and perhaps speeded up somewhat, so that the relationship between government and Indians could be redefined to truly reflect the needs of our native populations.
Our government is clearly committed to the eventual constitutional entrenchment of self-government. I mentioned in my opening remarks the prominence of the Meech Lake Accord at this particular time. Aboriginal rights are a key item for future meetings between the First Ministers and the government of this country.
While many problems must be addressed, there are optimistic signs for us. I feel quite optimistic that as we work together with our native population, we will bring about solutions to these problems.
In conclusion, let me say that human rights is not some abstract, theoretical concept to which lip-service must be paid. Rather, it is a real expression of the desire of people to be independent and in charge of their own lives and destinies. It is a wish to be treated with respect and fairness. The aboriginal people of Canada share these goals with us. They are something toward which we will work together.

This morning I reviewed with you, Mr. Speaker, some of the tragic and difficult situations that my constituents on Akwesasne have to live with in their everyday lives. I described the border issue.
Today during Question Period hon. colleagues were asking questions. One could tell that not everyone is familiar with the idea of how the border is situated and the difficulty in having access to Akwesasne and so on. That became obvious. It is a literal nightmare of jurisdiction.
I now want to turn to another subject, that being some of the difficulties that the people of Akwesasne have encountered in retaining their traditional way of life, or anything that resembles it.
First, the fact that they are partly in Ontario, partly in Quebec and partly in the New York state is difficult, at the best of times. Some years ago, the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority constructed a bridge between Canada and the United States at Cornwall. It was felt that the appropriate location for the bridge would be across Cornwall Island, therefore on the reserve of Akwesasne.
Although that bridge has been there since I was a little boy, the natives inform me that there is still a dispute over the amount of moneys owed to them by the federal government for placing the bridge there. As a matter of fact, they claim that they have yet to be paid for the location of that bridge which has been there for 30 years or more.
The people of Akwesasne, particularly those on Cornwall Island, for many years were farmers. Many of them were fishing guides and they worked well in that environment. I use the word "environment" advisedly.
As a result of the construction of the St. Lawrence Seaway, a number of factories established themselves in that area. On the American side there is a foundry known as General Foundry, which is a subsidiary of General Motors. Behind General Foundry, right on the banks of the St. Lawrence River, are these huge outdoor containers-they are actually large holes in the ground-in which there are toxic chemicals, right on the banks of the St. Lawrence River.
Immediately west of Akwesasne is the Alcoa plant, and right beside it is the Reynolds Aluminum plant. From the Reynolds plant, and possibly from the other one too, I am not sure, emissions of fluoride fall on the community of Akwesasne, particularly on Cornwall Island. It got so bad that approximately a decade ago the farmers of Cornwall Island had to get rid of their cattle. They were forced to slaughter the animals because the

Supply
milk given by the cows was contaminated and not fit for human consumption. The teeth of the children of Akwesasne were in awful condition as a result of the over-exposure to fluoride and that situation still exists.
I have a report here entitled "Phytotoxicology Investigations in the Cornwall area of Ontario in the vicinity of the Reynolds Metal Company and the Aluminum Company of America, Massena, New York". That report of 1988 says that the fall-out from those plants is still dangerous for human health today. This is about a decade after we came to the very sad conclusion of how this was affecting the lives of the people.
I said that the people of Akwesasne were also fishing guides and had a traditional way of life in that regard as well. You can imagine what that pollution in the St. Lawrence River has done to the fish and what it has done, of course, to the potential of being a fishing guide. So all in all we have severely damaged their way of life. And when I say "we" I mean we as a society. We have, of course, the crime rate and the other difficulties that I talked about earlier this morning which I will not repeat, and so on.
I would like to make the following point in conclusion. Outside the community of Akwesasne are all the good people who live around it. My constituents and others from the city of Cornwall, represented by my colleague from Stormont-Dundas, work in such positions as customs officers and so on. speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On debate, the hon. member for Halifax West-Halifax, sorry.

Mr. Speaker, just on that point I will say, before I begin my remarks, that the hon. member for Halifax West and I grew up on the same street, albeit a number of years apart. We are both Haligonians but as you, Mr. Speaker, are aware, we do have a different party affiliation.
I rise today to speak in strongest support of the motion moved by my colleague, the member for Winnipeg North Centre. I begin by quoting from that motion:
That this House reaffirm that all persons are equal under the law
and demand that the government (1) promote this fundamental
human right for Canada's aboriginal peoples-
There is more in the motion, as you are aware, but I would like to begin my remarks in this debate on this particular area.
My colleague from North Delta made some very interesting comments a few moments ago. He talked about the fact that Canadians can be proud of their human rights record and that people come from all over the world to make Canada their home because of this record. With the greatest of respect to my colleague, I think this has become a myth that too many Canadians
May 1, 1990

believe. It is a myth which examination of the facts in Canada show to be untrue.
We have perhaps a small problem in Canada in that we tend to be a little smug when we look at our neighbours to the south. We tend to think that because we are smaller, more spread out, because we have a history that has evolved into a democratic nation rather than being born through revolution, because we tend to be less violent, at least on the face of it, than our American cousins, that all of these things add up to a Canada that is somewhat better, more congenial to all peoples, less bigoted and less racist. The sad truth is that this is just not the case.
We do not have to look very far to see that this is not the case for people who are visible minorities. It is not the case for women. It is not the case for new Canadians in their first, second and even third generations. It is not the case at all and it is something about which Canadians have to do something.
I refer, first, to this year's report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. That report states that in a year that witnessed the fortieth anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the contrast between the ringing affirmation of human solidarity that that universal declaration gave and our common practice seems particularly harsh.
In relating it specifically to the question of Canada's first people, the report noted that the special committee of Parliament on Indian self-government recommended in 1983 that the federal government establish a new relationship with Indian first nations and that an essential element of this relationship be the recognition of Indian self-government.
This report was accepted by the government of the day in 1984. Later in that very year the new government agreed that aspects of self-government could and should be dealt with in the context of Indian land claim negotiations. Consequently, the report states that the issue today is not whether aboriginal people should have greater control over their own affairs, but the nature and the extent of that control.
We look at the problems besetting native Canadians and I think we have to hang our heads in shame. My province of Nova Scotia has been singled out, and to a degree rightly so, for its treatment of Donald Marshall
Supply
Jr. After many years, long hearings, much soul-searching, the royal commission known as the Marshall Inquiry was published earlier this year. That commission made 82 recommendations. Those recommendations covered a gambit of areas from criminal trial procedures to police investigations.
For the purposes of this motion it is important to note that the commission found that the fact that Marshall was a native was a factor in his wrongful conviction and imprisonment, that the immediate response to the death of Sandy Seal was entirely inadequate, incompetent and unprofessional and that the fact that Donald Marshall was a Micmac was one of the reasons that the police identified him as a prime suspect.
A further finding of the commission was that racism played a part in a wrongful conviction and imprisonment. Further recommendations were that the Department of the Attorney General and Solicitor General in Nova Scotia adopt and publicize a policy on race relations; that the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia, as well as the Nova Scotia bar, financially support Dalhousie Law School's new special minority admissions program for Micmacs and indigenous blacks; that there be law school programs for visible minorities and that training for police officers include discussion of minority issues and encourage sensitivity to minority concerns.
I might add that this, too, is mentioned in the report of the Human Rights Commission and that the Human Rights Commission notes in particular that this kind of training is now taking place in the RCMR But, Mr. Speaker, it must take in police forces nation-wide to prevent travesties of justice similar to that in the Donald Marshall case. Donald Marshall spent 11 years in penitentiary for a crime he did not commit. Nothing will give him back those 11 year. Nothing, except a completely new and fair attitude on the part of governments and on the part of people, will redress the wrong done to Canadian native peoples.
Further recommendations of the Marshall Inquiry are that a community controlled native criminal court be established in Nova Scotia; that a native justice institute be established with funding from both the federal and the provincial governments and that in Nova Scotia in particular Micmac interpreters be provided in all courts in the province.

May 1, 1990
Supply
One of the things noted in the report of the federal Human Rights Commission is that the evidence that native Canadians are over-represented in our prisons is inescapable. In a report prepared for the Canadian Bar Association in 1988 it was shown that 10 per cent of male inmates and 13 per cent of female inmates in Canadian federal penitentiaries are native, although native peoples make up only about 2 per cent of the general population.
The situation in provincial institutions is worse. In fact, it is a tragic but true situation that an Indian child born in this country has a far greater chance of going to penitentiary than he does of finishing university.
It was discovered in the course of the Marshall Inquiry that the lack of an interpreter for Donald Marshall at his initial trial, and even at his later hearing where he was finally cleared, was a major obstacle to his fair treatment by the court.
When I visited Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories some months ago I learned that one of the towns in the north-I am sorry, I forget which one-declared itself octolingual, to represent all of the languages spoken including, I might add, English and French, and six different native languages in that particular small town.
We can all learn from that kind of a gesture, particularly in the Canada of today, where so much tension, unhappiness and insensitivity is driving our nation to the brink of break-up because of a lack of a sensitivity by some of our people toward other of our people on the question of language.
If Donald Marshall had had an interpreter at his first trial in the early 1970s, I do not say that that would have made a major difference, given all the other problems, but it might have made his own time there a little easier. It might have turned up something that the courts would have had to listen to. It might have helped prevent the tragedy that then unfolded over the next 11 years.
The report also calls for public awareness programs. This, I think, is one of the areas of such great need,
where all of us can lead, because the problem almost goes beyond that of ordinary racism and ordinary bigotry.
Too many Canadians, vis-a-vis our native peoples have, not even a paternalism, which would be hard enough to accept, but a total ignorance, a total obliviousness to the fact that these are the indigenous people of Canada, that they have a specific culture, lifestyle and way of life that they have right to see continued, that they have a spiritual element that may be different from various other groups in this country but that is part and parcel and an integral part of their lifestyle which must be continued and respected by other Canadian citizens.
Until we see that in our schools, universities and other cultural institutions and on our television programs that sensitivity will not be created.
Bear in mind that everything that is stated regarding the province of Nova Scotia is equally true for every other province in the country and for the national government as well. Further recommendations of the Marshall Inquiry were that the Chief Justices and Chief Judges of each court in Nova Scotia should exercise leadership to ensure fair treatment of minorities within the system, that provincial funding to legal aid be re-examined to better serve the needs of minority clients and that municipal police departments and the RCMP actively recruit minorities.
Again, as part of the sensitivity and the training of police forces natives must be hired in these police forces and have input into the manner in which their people and they themselves are dealt with by these forces. A further recommendation was that official policies on the elimination of racial stereotypes be developed by all levels of government.
Nobody would stand up in this House and deny the need for any of these things. Nobody would stand up and deny the need for any of these programs. Nobody would stand up in this House and suggest that the status of native people in this country is anything that we can be proud of, that the treatment of native people by newer Canadians such as ourselves is anything that we should be prepared to boast about.
The time has come for action, the time has come for specific programs, but that is not what we are seeing. What we have seen, on the other hand, is the cancellation of the native communication programs.
While Donald Marshall was languishing in the federal penitentiary in Dorchester, New Brunswick, there was
May 1, 1990

one champion for his innocence, one champion that worked on and on all during his incarceration to see justice done. I refer, of course, to the Micmac News. The Micmac News has been published in Nova Scotia for over 20 years. It has a circulation among native people and others of over 4,800 and it has done a tremendous amount of good. It has been a source of communication and pride to the Micmac community in Atlantic Canada and it is the only major native newspaper in Atlantic Canada. Mr. Speaker, its federal funding has been cut.
This is a tragedy. It is more than just a tragedy in the sense of a loss of a communication instrument for native people. For native people in Atlantic Canada who know that the Micmac News was so much a first cause in the final freeing of Donald Marshall there is a fear that the reason it has been cut is a deliberate move-I do not suggest this, Mr. Speaker, but among native people the feeling is it is a deliberate move to silence a voice that has done some good for native people.
The attitude among young native people in my region is that the white man's government is not relevant to them, that the white man's government does not care about them and that empty promises, broken promises and paternalistic feeling do nothing but cause amusement and despair. The amusement we might be able to do something about, but the despair goes right to the root of the lives of desperation that people live because they do not have the wherewithal to make it in a society that forever shunts them to the side.
Donald Marshall is the example to which we can all point. We know about Donald Marshall, we know what has happened to him and we know what it has meant to his life to have 11 years taken away from him, 11 years from the age of 17 to 28 when he would have been being educated, learning a trade and starting his lifelong career.
Native Canadians right across the country are suffering every day. They are suffering because our society puts little or no value on their contribution, because our society refuses to understand that the way they live their lives is as important and as relevant to the great cultural fabric of this country as the way those of us of Irish, English, French or Polish descent live our lives. It has to stop. It has to stop by a concerted effort of government
Supply
to follow the kinds of recommendations that the Marshall Inquiry has suggested.
As I already mentioned, we see in Canada today a disproportionate number of natives in prison. Interestingly enough, the figure is even more disproportionate for native women than for native men. We see a disproportionate alcoholism rate, a disproportionate unemployment rate and a disproportionate suicide rate. All of these things lead us to see that the overwhelming spirit in the native community, if we do not act to right these wrongs and redress these wrongs as soon as humanly possible, is despair.
Canada is not a country that should engender despair in any of its people. Canada is a country that should engender hope for the future with a pride in the past, a pride in the past from our native peoples who were here when we got here. If we do not take care of this country the way we should, they will still be here after we have gone.
I can only add my voice to that of my colleagues from Winnipeg North Centre, Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, Stormont-Dundas and others who have spoken and will speak today and say to this government and to all of us here in Canada: for God's sake do something, act on these recommendations, show that our government and our country is not callous and uncaring, show that our government and our country puts a premium on all its people wherever they live, whatever their background and, most particularly, on our native people.

Mr. Speaker, I do not have a question for the hon. member but I would like to add my voice to the debate in this comment period.
I agree with the member's analysis that the fundamental problem is a complete lack of hope. I have long been interested in this. In fact I did an honours paper at university on the history of the Indian franchise in British Columbia so I have a demonstrated interest in that. Now that I am the member of Parliament for Saanich-Gulf Islands I have tried to reach out to the native communities in my district. I am finding that they feel very apart and outside of the mainstream of political activity.

May 1, 1990
Supply
There is a very real fundamental mistrust of federal or provincial politicians to in any way address their requirements. I think that that is an historical mistrust. We have never been able to give them the kind of representation that they feel they require. I think there is this fundamental mistrust because we do not understand and also because of the kind of hurts that have been generated over history. Many of the comments by my colleague from Comox-Alberni this morning speak to that fundamental mistrust and the reasons for it.
I would like to reiterate what he said about that. If we are going to get real treatment for native justice in Canada we have to focus on the fundamentals. They are three: The first is constitutional recognition. We now have a constitutional crisis in our country. It is because, I believe, of the lack of consultation with ordinary people. The politicians felt more able and adept at handling constitutional matters than ordinary people and this is what we have. got. We have a mess.
The second item in recognizing the fundamental problem of native people is land claims. EIow can we give people the kind of recognition and respect that they deserve if we do not even recognize that they were here first and have some sense of ownership and some sense of responsibility to their land. They did it a whole lot better than many of us. Sitting on the environment committee, I have listened to members of many tribes speak of the kind of reverence they have for their environment. We could learn from them, Mr. Speaker, and we are not doing a very good job of that.
Finally, as my colleague from Comox-Alberni has pointed out, what we should be doing is strengthening human rights legislation. As the member from Halifax points out, we have a reputation but sometimes one wonders whether that reputation is well deserved or not. They say you cannot legislate morality. You can make sure that cases such as Donald Marshall will never happen again. For those people crying out for the renewal of capital punishment, Donald Marshall is certainly a case in point where the fundamental inhumanity dealt to this person from a native community would not have occurred if he were not a native.
My task as a member of Parliament in trying to represent all of my constituents is to build those bridges
of communication and to try to speak to people and get them to trust so that they can tell us what they want us to do as their representatives.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Saanich-Gulf Islands for her comments. I would like to add to what she has said when she mentioned, in particular, the subject of human rights. There are two points, Mr. Speaker.
One is the need for promotion of human rights vehicles and the response through provincial and federal human rights commissions in native communities. There is very little awareness and it has certainly given the federal government responsibility for first people. I think it is a policy which could be acted upon and acted upon quickly to promote the use of human rights commissions through the native communities in this country.
The second comment I would like to make in response to my colleague's comments relates to a situation that arose again out of the Marshall case that I heard in Nova Scotia. There was a civil suit that arose from some of the goings on in the Marshall Inquiry. The lawyer involved told me that he had asked a young native Nova Scotian to testify. The young man said to him: "Why, what good will it do? It never works for us. The system does not work for us, it only works against us." My friend tried and tried to convince him that the system could work for him. This young man, who I think was every day of 22-tragically the same age as that young man who died today at Akwesasne-said: "No, I am sorry; I do not believe you. I have no faith in your system; it will never do me any good". We cannot continue to allow this to be the case in our country.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a couple of short comments. This is a subject that moves me a lot because I have had the opportunity, in the past, as a journalist and as a broadcaster to do several documentaries about the Indian community and the problems related to our aboriginals in this country. My friend, the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands, talked about mistrust and misunderstanding, and it is the absolute truth.
One of the problems we have, and it is a very complex matter, is that we simply just do not know each other. We do not work with each other. There are a lot of middle-class, white Canadians in this country who will offer gratuituous comments about Indians and yet they

May 1, 1990

have never worked with them, befriended them or been with them, or ever been on a reserve.
Actually-and it is unfortunate in many ways-it is not normal for a lot of Canadians to have native Indians come into their lives every day, every week, or every month. In fact, I suspect there are many, many, if not millions of Canadians who have never shaken hands with a native Indian and it would do them well to do it. They should visit Indian reserves in northern Manitoba, northwestern Ontario and Saskatchewan, as I have. It would be an eye-opener. They would realize that these are human beings who want to live in peace, who want to prosper, who want to get ahead, and who have feelings like the rest of us.
It is something that moves you and hurts you a lot when you visit a reserve and discover that perhaps, in the winter time, 95 per cent of the adults, men and women, are unemployed and perhaps in the summer time it may go down to 70 per cent or 80 percent. That is how shocking it is. The problem is enormous.
Yes, there is a constitutional crisis; yes, we have to deal with land claims; and yes, we have to deal with some of these issues that are in the news all the time, but I would suggest that at the root of it is this mistrust and this misunderstanding and all of us, including the government of the day, should do something to help us get to know each other better.

Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate, but before I recognize the hon. member for South Shore-

It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Chambly-Women's Centres; the hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap-The Environment; the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon-Pearson International Airport.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this debate this afternoon. I am particularly pleased to speak
Supply
following my good friend, the hon. member for Halifax. I rarely follow my hon. friend but I am always pleased to speak after her in debate, and today is no exception to that.
I wish to begin by commending the hon. member for Winnipeg North for bringing forth this very important set of issues relating to human rights in Canada and, indeed, relating to native people.
It is curious that he mentioned privately to me, when we were speaking a few minutes ago, the coincidence that today should be the day for this debate when we have, in fact, seen such a tragic event in Canada and North America relating to native people and, indeed, to the administration of justice on both sides of the border. I wish to commend him for bringing this issue forth because what we are talking about here today is, fundamentally, human rights. Issues of human rights are really issues which are non-partisan. They are issues that are of concern to all members of this House, I am sure, and they are of concern to all Canadians because, as Canadians, we value very highly our concept of our country as a democratic country.
The equality of Canadians, which is so much a part of the ethic of Canadian society and indeed a part of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, is something that we must continuously pursue until such time as we can be satisfied that it exists in practice throughout our country before the courts, before the police and in terms of access as well as opportunity to participate fully in all aspects of Canadian life.
Increasingly over the next decade we are going to see issues such as the issues that we are dealing with today become more and more in the forefront of Canadian consideration. Our society is changing at a phenomenal rate, and it will continue to change at a phenomenal rate because of the immigration needs of Canada. It is inevitable that we will continue to see the development of our population as a multiracial population. Issues such as whether or not people who may be different by virtue of their skin colour, their culture, their language, their religion or other aspects of their cultural heritage may find themselves in the position where they are not treated equally as Canadians. That is something that we

Supply
must all seek to eradicate in order that our country will live up to the principles articulated in our Constitution.
Native people in Canada are in a particularly unique position as compared to other persons who might be referred to as minorities in Canada. Quite simply, others who have come here as immigrants have chosen to come. They recognized when they left their homelands that they may face circumstances that are different, and that they may have challenges beyond those which they might face if they stayed at home. This is not the case with native people, because this is their ancestral home and the place where they should quite legitimately more than any other Canadians be able to call their homeland.
At the same time, when we talk about equality of Canadians sometimes I have had people say to me: "Why is it that native people have special status? Why is it that we talk about the equality of all Canadians, but yet native people have special privileges that other Canadians do not have, recognized in the Indian Act or elsewhere?" Quite simply, native people do not have special status in Canada. They are equal and pro-Canadians.
I noticed in my hon. friend's motion that there was something with which I wanted to take issue. In the motion he refers to the security of aboriginal people "who are entitled to the status of Canadian citizens". Native persons are Canadian citizens, full and equal with all other Canadians but they do enjoy benefits that other Canadians do not enjoy that relate to their special inheritance, in particular as status Indians as recognized through our law, Constitution and our traditions.
These special privileges that I often hear people criticize, one should remember, are no different than the inheritance that any other Canadian receives from his or her parents or ancestors, in the same way that my father may leave me certain of his property, rights or privileges when he passes on. Similarly, native people have legitimate right to receive from their ancestors certain rights and privileges that may accrue. Our goal must be to recognize all Canadians as equal under the law of Canada, and this is an aspiration that we must pursue.
My hon. friend from Halifax made reference to and spoke very sensitively on the subject of the recent Marshall inquiry in our province. There is no question
that that was a landmark, a very important investigation in the history of this country, and in the history of the administration of justice. I read that report with fascination. It was one of the most interesting documents of its sort that I have read in a long time. It was absolutely captivating reading and made some very valuable and important recommendations for our society.
I have said previously on a Standing Order 31 in this House and would say again today that Canadians from other provinces should not be smug about the Marshall report. Perhaps my hon. friend from Halifax has had people say to her: "What's your problem there in Nova Scotia?" The fact is it is not our problem there in Nova Scotia. Inquiries could be held in other provinces that could reveal the same problems with respect to the administration of justice, or possibly the administration of other public institutions in our society.
We happen to be in a position in Nova Scotia where we have now had the definitive evidence of a problem that we have to come to grips with in Nova Scotia. I am pleased to see the quick response of the Government of Nova Scotia to that. I am also pleased to see that the Minister of Justice for Canada and her officials have been reviewing the recommendations of the Marshall report to see if there are implications for the Government of Canada, and if they would identify needs on our part to change the way things are done nationally.
I would expect, as well, that the forthcoming report of the Manitoba aboriginal justice inquiry will also give us an opportunity for further insights and understanding in this whole area. I think we can expect that the dialogue is only just beginning at a very serious level in Canada. I think people could argue quite legitimately that perhaps it is overdue. Nevertheless, the dialogue is well under way.
The motion by the hon. member for Winnipeg North demands that the government "pursue alternative aboriginal justice initiatives". I am pleased to say that this government is deeply concerned about the native justice issues and is engaged in a number of initiatives in this area, some of which I would like to mention briefly today. First, I would like to provide a context for the discussion before addressing the specific initiatives which the government has undertaken.
May 1, 1990

By its nature the justice system deals with conflicts between individuals, between individuals and the state, and between groups. Accordingly the issues discussed here tend to focus on problems, concerns about abuses and wrongs done. It is, however, necessary to approach the development of responses to these problems positively. It is necessary to focus on the evolution of a system of justice that is meaningful for all Canadians, to search for laws, procedures and institutions that exist through the free consent of all citizens regardless of culture or race.
One of the areas of concern to native people in Canada is the provision of policing services on reserves, something of which we have been very much aware in the last week or two in this country. The importance of policing services in the development of effective justice administration is reflected in the fact that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development undertook a review of Indian reserve policing to canvass the variety of present policing arrangements, examine the question of jurisdiction and assess alternative models.
These efforts which involve national consultations seek to ensure that Indian communities have access to appropriate kinds and levels of policing services. In January 1990 the final report on reserve policing was released publicly, and I understand consultations with interested parties are anticipated to be completed later this year.
As previously noted, aboriginal offenders are disproportionately represented in prisons. The ministry of the Solicitor General responsible for federal correctional services has taken special effort to identify programs and services that will ensure that programs and institutions are responsive to aboriginal concerns and needs. These efforts have often been undertaken in consultation with aboriginal organizations and groups, and encourage the active participation of native communities.
The correctional law review process and the task force report on the reintegration of the aboriginal offender both point to the commitment of developing programs in dialogue with aboriginal communities. The administration of justice is one of the matters that may be discussed in aboriginal self-government negotiations. In preparation, the Department of Justice led an interdepartmental
Supply
committee to develop principles to guide the negotiations. This is part of the government's ongoing commitment to the concept of aboriginal self-government.
All members should be aware that the government and this minister are receptive to initiatives developed by the aboriginal communities themselves. I might say that for the first year and a half that I had the privilege to be a member of this place, I dealt a great deal with the minister who is now the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I found that as Minister of Fisheries and Oceans he was one of the most approachable ministers of the government, and I can see that he is off to an outstanding beginning as Minister of Indian Affairs in having concluded some absolutely landmark agreements in the history of this country. There is no doubt in my mind as to his receptiveness.
The Department of Justice provides funding in a variety of aboriginal justice areas. In addition to proposals for radical institutional reforms such as would be implied by proposals for separate tribal courts and similar mechanisms, aboriginal communities and organizations have proposed a wide array of alternative program models. Various other proposals have relied upon mediation and arbitration schemes which, being consen-tual in nature, only work if the parties voluntarily participate. These may offer wide scope for accommodating the particular values and traditions of the community.
In conclusion, it would be difficult, even inappropriate, to attempt to identify all the alternatives that might be available to Canadians in this area. At this time, we can only agree that alternatives to existing processes, as well as improvements to the existing ones, are at the heart of long-term solutions.
As the government explores new approaches, whether in the community self-government negotiations, the renewed constitutional discussions, law reform initiatives or elsewhere, the participation of aboriginal Canadians will ensure that appropriate alternatives are considered and the human rights principles that characterize our system of justice are advanced for all Canadians.

Questions or comments? Debate, the hon. member for Regina- Qu'Appelle. It is a 10-minute debate and five minutes

May 1, 1990
Supply
for questions or comments. You are splitting it with the hon. member for Victoria?

I am, Mr. Speaker, and thank you very much.
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me today to join in the debate on the motion of the Official Opposition regarding an Indian justice system. In my constituency of Regina-Qu'Appelle, I have over 11 Indian reserves. Most of them are Cree, although I do have some Sioux. As well, that part of Regina which I represent has a fair number of urban Indian people, not just treaty people, but also Metis and non-treaty people.
I have been a friend, an observer, and an associate of the native community back home for a number of years. As a new Canadian, a person whose family came to this country not too many years ago, I have to acknowledge the original people in this country, the Indian people. The fact that I now represent them in this House of Parliament, I feel, puts a special responsibility on my shoulders.
We have heard many members speak eloquently in this House today about the plight of the Indian people. We have heard about the statistics. Back in my own province of Saskatchewan, some 36 per cent of the inmates in the federal penitentiary are native people; in the provincial penitentiary, over 85 per cent of the inmates are of native ancestry. People of native ancestry only constitute 16 per cent of the Saskatchewan population.
When we consider the social statistics such as marriage breakdown, alcoholism, life expectancy, the rate of death by violent means, housing conditions on reserves, the unemployment rate, one has to come away with a sad heart and say that this is indeed the worst of Third World conditions.
Yet, I think it would be wrong for us not to also see some positive things. We can stand and lay blame that goes back many, many years, to the paternalistic attitude that previous governments have taken. It was not until toward the end of the 1950s that a band could sell a cow without having to receive the approval of the Indian, agent who had to get the approval from Ottawa.
If there was ever an indictment of over-welfare, certainly the Department of Indian Affairs and our treatment of Indian people is that example. We never
gave them an opportunity to be responsible for their own lives. Some of that is beginning to change. We see positive developments in terms of developing educational institutions on the reserves, manned and operated by the bands. We are beginning to see some economic agreements between the bands and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development that are beginning to allow for some economic development. We are beginning to see bands taking over the administration of social services, housing, and these other programs on the reserves themselves.
We, as members of parliament, should be encouraging these developments because, in the end, people having responsibility over their own lives is what it is really all about. Let the Indian people regain responsibility over their own lives. It is in this way that the Indian people will regain for themselves their own sense of pride. If there is one thing that the white civilization has done to our Indian brothers and sisters over the years is to take away their pride.
We almost destroyed them as a people, but as I mentioned earlier there are some hopeful signs that Indian pride is coming back. Every year I attend powwows on my reserves and in the 11 years that I have been a member of parliament I have seen these powwows grow not only in terms of numbers of people participating in them but also in the rebirth of Indian spiritualism that accompanies their renewed sense of pride. I see it in the faces of the young men and women going to the powwows on those reserves. I see that this Indian spiritualism is being used to combat problems like alcoholism on the reserve. They are beginning to get back their pride, which is essential if we really are concerned about the welfare of the Indian people.
The other area that needs serious attention is the native justice system. The opposition motion today deals with that question. Again we see some positive things. Toward the end of last year I had the honour and the privilege of participating in a ceremony in the town of Fort Qu'Appelle which started a training program for young Indian and Metis boys and girls who were going to enter the program to become Indian special constables in the RCMP.
I have to acknowledge the role that the RCMP has been taking. The RCMP is beginning to realize that they
May 1, 1990

need native constables, especially if they are going to be dealing with the question of policing the reserves.
Much more needs to be done. All those programs are under-funded. There are more young Indian people wanting to apply to those programs than there are openings. I think about the Saskatchewan Indian Cultural College. Again we are seeing young Indian men and women wanting to advance their education and yet, unfortunately, the funding is being cut off to those important programs.
We have heard some of the possible solutions in speeches today. One of the most important ways to solve the problems that Indian people are facing is to resolve the land question. We have not lived up to commitments that previous governments have made to the Indian people. In fact in many instances we have stolen land from the Indian people. We have ignored legal agreements that we have made. In the past, crooked Indian agents have swindled Indian bands and Indian people out of their rightful land. This has got to be corrected.
Land settlements will begin to create an economic base that would allow the Indian people to develop a self-sustaining economy within their bands, thereby providing employment, and setting positive models for the Indian people.
The second area that I believe is important is education. We cannot and should not deny education opportunities to the young Indian men and women. People without pride lack positive role models. We are beginning to see positive role models developing in the Indian community. These are young men and women who have done exceptionally well at post-secondary education, very often against tremendous odds. Very often they do not have the white support or the family support in the urban setting.
Many of these young Indian men and women come from the reserves directly into an urban centre where they usually do not have the support system they need. They have to combat the temptation to become involved in the down side of urban Indian living is there. They have to combat the pressures and the newness of a white university system. Very often they are not adequately trained in terms of their past high school record so they need special help and attention as well.
Supply
Those young Indian men and women who have come through the system with their degrees are really people whom we should all admire. They are the positive role models. They are the future for the Indian people.
If there is anything I can do in this House in terms of my appeal to government members, it would be to ensure that funding for post-secondary education to native young men and women not be curtailed, that we give them every opportunity of availing themselves of post-secondary education, because that is where the future lies.
The third area which is important is the area that the Official Opposition has raised. We need a justice system that is sensitive to Indian needs and Indian values. To this end, I sincerely urge the government to give the matter serious consideration, not just lip-service, to ensure that a system will evolve that will indeed provide justice to our Indian brothers and sisters.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for his excellent comments and for contributing to this very important debate.
The final issue he raised is one which I think deserves to be elaborated on. In western Canada several organizations are thinking about alternative justice systems. There seems to be a reluctance on the part of the federal government to get involved in a debate on this issue. Yet we all know that tribal councils, provincial organizations and individual bands are seeking ways of increasing their participation rate and their control over these systems. In Manitoba the Aboriginal Justice Committee had a very important two-day conference on this issue, and Alberta is considering it in the course of its own investigations.
Perhaps the member from Regina could further contribute to the debate by elaborating on the need for alternative justice systems to be more responsive to the native communities that we find particularly in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, yes, indeed, I agree. When we talk about a justice system, we should also talk about the need for more law enforcement officers of native ancestry. We need people of native ancestry to be judges

May 1, 1990
Supply
and members of tribunals. We need Indian lawyers as well.
If, indeed, our system of justice is to meet the needs of the native community, then these things must be in place. Without them there will be discrimination and racism, either overt or not. Policemen and judges, because of their upbringing and their attitudes, may unconsciously be racist or prejudiced since they do not very often understand the forces involved in a native's life.
When I returned to Saskatchewan in the 1970s and worked in the office of the Minister of Social Services, there was an attempt by young natives in Regina to have a young native police force. The official establishment, the police department and the welfare agencies were quick to denounce this. Yet it had some merit.
They were proposing that when, for example, Indian people went on a binge, instead of picking them up and throwing them in jail they would exercise wisdom and just gently take them home. That, to me, was wisdom. That was dealing with a problem in a wise way, rather than the way the white society deals with them. That is to say, when they find people who are inebriated on the streets they throw them in the paddy wagon and throw them in the cell.
If they are Indian.

That is right, if they are Indians
There are other, more wise ways of dealing with these questions. They should come from the Indian community. I thank the hon. member for his question.

speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. On debate, the hon. member for Victoria. He also has 10 minutes of debate plus five minutes for questions and comments .

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this important debate. To refresh the House as to the motion before it, it states:
That this House reaffirm that all persons are equal under the law and demand that the government (1) promote this fundamental human right for Canada's aboriginal peoples, (2) ensure that our system of justice is more responsive and suitable, (3) pursue alternative aboriginal justice initiatives, and (4) in cases of jurisdictional conflict, that the Government of Canada, in consultation with aboriginal leaders, ensure the protection of the life, liberty, and security of aboriginal people who are entitled to the status of Canadian citizens.
This motion permits us to deal with a number of issues which are current in Canada, starting with the issue that is current today, that is, the tragedy at the Mohawk reserve on the Canadian border, where the Canadian government, having had representations from the responsible elected and traditional leaders, has failed to respond. As a result, a tragedy has ensued.
It is important that the Canadian government respond to the leadership of the native people, not only in that community but the national leadership who have joined in that request, and deal promptly and fairly with our citizens on the reserve in that tragedy.
The motion takes us beyond that particular issue into what is really one of the searing injustices in this country'. That is an injustice which has its roots in our history. I found that for me it was a gradual process of beginning to understand the depths and nature of the tragedy which we see about us today.
Before the Europeans came aboriginal people had a society which, while it was different in different parts of the continent, was generally marked by cohesion, by political stability, by a spirituality and cultural integration with the community and with the environment that we would all be pleased to have today in North America.
The impact of European intervention in North America has proven to be a disaster for most aboriginal people. Lisa Hobbs Birnie, who has written a very recently published book on the life and work of the National Parole Board, and others have described the relationship today as that of a Third World country living in the midst of one of the richest societies that history has ever known.
It is that first point which needs to be understood by non-aboriginal Canadians. That is to say that the culture and life that was here when the Europeans first arrived still remains in some fashion, and has not been absorbed within the European culture. Thus, daily, we have a clash of cultures, of worlds, that are radically different. This is caught up and described in the statistics. Perhaps we non-aboriginal people need statistics to help us understand the nature of the problem.
Not only are living standards dramatically lower across this country for aboriginal people, but social problems that arise because of a constant bombardment of their culture create a horror story in many areas of the native community. That horror story gets itself acted out in a
May 1, 1990

clash with our system of justice. That clash shows up at every point in the administration of justice. It shows up in tensions with the police, as we have seen in the evidence that has come out of the Manitoba inquiry, and in the Donald Marshall case where a police force which is essentially non-aboriginal and which struggles to try to understand the culture that it is dealing with is usually at a complete disadvantage.
Many of our police officers-the RCMP as an institution, and the provincial police forces-have learned more than most of us about the tragedies and how to deal with them. But one of the great problems is that their voices are not being listened to in the council of government.
Since I have been here, and I have been critic for the Solicitor General's department, I have been visited with more reports than one could imagine on this subject. I have in my hand a report on policing for aboriginal Canadians, and the RCMP role in it.
My friend from Regina outlined a number of steps that could be taken. Each page has a series of specific recommendations which the police would like to bring into practice across this country which would only begin to deal with part of the problem.
I also have a copy of the report of the Indian Policing Policy Review Task Force which involved a number of departments. Again, it contains a series of recommendations which would begin to deal with the difficulties of policing at that level, on the reserves and in our cities.
The next level of the system is the courts. There are very few lawyers who are native. There are very few lawyers who have even had any education or training in native or aboriginal culture. There are very few judges who have had such training.
When I was with the Attorney General's Department in British Columbia, we had a program which taught us a few things. We picked up something from Saskatchewan which I thought was very helpful and instructive. It is something that the lawyers, prosecutors and judges were put through. They put native people on the bench and in the role of lawyers. They put the lawyers and judges in the role of the accused and the witnesses. They conducted the whole trial in Cree, with translators. That
Supply
gave to those people a sense of the dramatic cultural impact, confusion and difficulty that the court system has.
Again, the Marshall Inquiry has underlined how that kind of injustice can happen in this country. Donald Marshall is just one case in thousands upon thousands in the history of this country.
I now come to corrections. Again, we have a task force report on corrections which has everybody's name on it. It has page after page after page of recommendations. It came out in 1988.
We had the chairman of the Parole Board in front of the justice committee today. We had the commissioner of corrections there last week. The week before that we had the Solicitor General. However, these recommendations are being implemented at a snail's pace.
It is little wonder that native people and aboriginal people are now beginning to be angry at what is happening. Perhaps out of some of that anger will finally come a hearing for the native people.
This report reveals that aboriginal Canadians take longer to get parole than non-aboriginal Canadians. Their sentences are longer. Even when they do get parole they have spent more time in jail. Their recidivism rate is higher.
That is because our system has failed. We have almost no programs in our jails for drug addiction or for alcohol treatment. We have almost no programs sensitive to the cultural traditions of native people.
Last week we received a report on creating choices. It is a report of the Thsk Force on Federally Sentenced Women. If you think it is bad in this country for a federally sentenced woman, try being a federally sentenced native woman in our institutions.
This report speaks with the cry of pain that native women feel. Because we have only one institution in this country for women, they are dragged from their homes in the north, or in Saskatchewan or Alberta to a jail in Kingston, Ontario-a jail that was built in 1933 and condemned in 1938.
That is what we have been inflicting native women with. They commit suicide as a result. Just a few months ago there was yet another suicide in the prison for women.

Yet, when we ask the commissioner of corrections and the Solicitor General for a clear commitment to the principles of this report we get: "Well, we will have to think about it. We will have to look at our options. We have got all these other priorities. We will have to see".
The time has come for this House to speak with one voice on this issue. The voice must be that the time has come for action for our native people in the area of administrative justice. They need not look to this House further than today for a clear statement that we stand with them in their plea for justice.
We want to hear from the next speaker, the Minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, that this government is finally going to deal in a clear, honest and upfront way with the cries of native people. We want to hear that, finally, the injustices that have been perpetrated on those people for too long are going to come to an end, and that we will together begin to address the issues that these reports speak of and that we in this House want dealt with now.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague on his excellent dissertation on the effects of the justice system on our native population. I certainly think he has emphasized some of its shortcomings.
I do have a question for him. I was a little concerned with some of the things he was talking about when he spoke of sending in the RCMP to the Akwesasne reserve on a unilateral basis.
I wish to read from an article which appeared in this morning's The Globe and Mail. It quotes the Governor of New York State.
Again, we need to recognize that this is a multiple level problem with the Canadian and U.S. governments, as well as the governments of Quebec, Ontario and New York State. All of these jurisdictions are involved.
The article states that the Governor of New York State said: "there is a time for the use of military force" but only after all other avenues leading toward a peaceful resolution have been explored.
Mr. Clark is quoted as having said:
Much of the source of the problem in our view is on the U.S. side.
Our expectation is that the Americans on a state and a national level
will also play an effective role to resolve this as quickly and peacefully
as possible.
My question is this. Is it not rather dangerous to send our police into a situation where they could be fired at with impunity across the border? If we started to fire back at them, or if they were in any way to protect themselves, we would soon have an international incident.
I believe this is a time for all levels of government to get together and to come to a solution. It is not the time for Canada to take action unilaterally, as was indicated.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend for the question.
We have an international incident on our hands right now. The issue is not whether the RCMP should go in unilaterally. The responsible elected and traditional leaders of the reserve have asked that the RCMP come in and bring law and order to that situation.
Frankly, we can all slip into something of a cultural response which says that only when the local police force is asked will we regard that as a legitimate request. But here we have the legitimate authority on the reserve asking that the RCMP come in.
I may add as well that the key issue is which police force is going to be responsible for dealing with it. I do not purport to advocate that the RCMP should necessarily take any particular steps to bring about law and order. That is a decision that it should make. But the RCMP should be put clearly in charge of the situation, and it should be up to it to decide what are the appropriate police steps to be taken.
A native person today described the situation to me like this. Quebec police are on the Quebec part of the reserve. Ontario police on the Ontario part of the reserve. The RCMP is going around in boats.
It seems to me that the time has come for our national police force to move into that situation and use its judgment as to the best policing methods.
Let me conclude by trading editorials. My friend referred to The Globe and Mail of Toronto. The Ottawa Sun, a journal of great wisdom and perception on



May 1, 1990

occasions-perhaps rare-had it right on this occasion. It stated today in an editorial headed "Native land":
North American Indians often accuse the white establishment of meddling in their affairs -except when the interference is really needed.
On the basis of the uproar on the Akwesasne Reserve, no doubt about it, the Indians are right.
It goes on to state that the trouble is that there are too many officials.
So far the best most of them have been able to do is dither. Meanwhile, the 9,000 members of the reserve are, in effect, being held hostage by the Warriors Society based -in the reserve's New York sector.
New York State officials keep saying controversy over the half dozen casinos is entirely a Mohawk problem. This is the coward's approach.
The attitude enrages Canadian Indian leader George Erasmus who says there's no other group in either country that authorities would leave in such a predicament. He adds: "Canada has got to act".
As Joe Clark said yesterday, the situation is "near anarchy".
The editorial concludes:
He's right. We must act. Indeed, the Mounties and FBI owe it to the Mohawks to help maintain the peace on their reserve. If they wait until lives are lost, they will share the guilt for the deaths.
