speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to the motion currently before the House in the name of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
In doing so I know that there is a great sense of sadness, and certainly tremendous sympathy, for the family of the young Mohawk person who was this morning killed in a violent incident on the Akwesasne Reserve near Cornwall.
I want to begin by commending the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in his concern for the basic human rights of aboriginal peoples. The motion before us focuses on the importance of recognizing that all persons are equal under the law but, at the same time, the responsibility of this federal government and all institutions of Canada is to promote the fundamental human rights of Canada's aboriginal peoples.
Supply
The motion further focuses on the impact of our justice system on Canadian natives and calls for the government to ensure the protection, liberty and security of aboriginal people.
I want to assure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others present in this House that I share his concerns, as do all members of the House. I am personally committed to pursuing initiatives in each of the areas covered in the motion.
I rather regret the focus of the remarks by the previous speaker from Victoria who has just resumed his seat. They were all in a relatively negative vein and did not recognize the very significant progress that this government has achieved since 1984 in the resolution of important aboriginal questions and a move toward greater self-reliance, the completion of comprehensive agreements and specific claims and the improvements, although totally inadequate, but nonetheless significant, in the living conditions our native people experience in the various regions of Canada.
I am personally committed to making significant further progress in these areas in the footsteps of my three predecessors in this government since 1984.
I want to thank my colleague, the hon. Minister of State and member of Parliament for Lincoln, for her part in supporting this work and in working to these same objectives with myself, but in particular for her leadership over the past few days in regard to the Akwesasne situation while I was away in Igloolik in the Northwest Territories for an historic and widely celebrated conclusion of the largest land claim in Canada's history. I will return to that very important occasion in a few moments.
The hon. member for Lincoln should be commended for her efforts over the past few days, as should the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and other members from surrounding constituencies. They should be commended for the leadership they have taken and for the calm and wise approach in judgment that they are bringing to bear as we seek a solution, now even more important, to this serious problem in the Akwesasne community.
My colleague from Lincoln yesterday visited the government training centre in Cornwall and spoke with many of the representatives of the Akwesasne community who voluntarily left the St. Regis community site on the south side of the St. Lawrence River, a small portion of peninsula on the south side of the St. Lawrence River,

May 1, 1990
Supply
but nonetheless a part of Canada. These people left their community with the assistance of Canadian enforcement agencies to seek shelter from the violence that has been brought into their midst by an element emanating from the New York State side of the reservation which is associated with the pro-gambling forces in that area.
It has been a trying time for all concerned, particularly so in light of today's disturbing events. It is not merely I, but all members of the House and all Canadians who are disturbed and saddened by the events and the death this morning of a young man.
As I said earlier, we want to extend our sympathies and those of all Canadians to the family and friends of this young Mohawk man who lost his life as a result of the senseless violence that continues there.
I have been informed by the RCMP, who learned earlier today from the Quebec provincial police force that 22-year old Matthew Pyke died at 10.57 a.m. this morning in hospital as a result of gunshot wounds. Mr. Pyke, who is a resident of Hogansburg, New York, was shot on the Canadian side, in Quebec at Snye, and was taken to a hospital in upstate New York for treatment where we ultimately expired.
I am dismayed that the situation has deteriorated to this point. One death is one death too many. I am sure all members of the House knowing how potentially explosive this issue is would want the government and all agencies to react with good judgment so as to ensure there will be no further loss of life and that we contain the violence and seek a mediated peaceful process for reversing this unfortunate situation.
The event of this morning only reinforces the urgency for all jurisdictions to recognize their obligation to maintain peace and order in the Akwesasne community. I will return to Akwesasne a little later.
On another front I would like to report that we have been making outstanding progress in the area of land claims to the benefit of our aboriginal people these past several months. In fact I would hazard to suggest that in the last two months we have had more significant progress in magnitude and in impact in resolving long
remaining injustices and a lack of proper legal settlement than we have seen in this entire century.
I have just returned in the early hours this morning from Igloolik, which is way up on the western limb of Hudson Bay in the Northwest Territories, near Baffin Island. I was there for the historic signing of the agreement in principle with the Tungavik Federation of the Nunavut, an agreement which has been sought now for some 14 years and on which significant progress has only been possible as a result of a new comprehensive claims policy introduced by my colleague, the now Minister of National Defence, in 1987.
It was a matter of great pride and personal satisfaction for me to be associated with this settlement. I want to personally compliment the Tungavik Federation of the Nunavut and its president for the vision, confidence, trust and generosity that they have shown toward Canada in agreeing to this settlement.
The settlement provides the 17,000 Inuit living in the region with $580 million in compensation funding over the next 15 years and confirms their title to over 350,000 square kilometres of land, an area of about half the size of Saskatchewan, and a portion of the larger Inuit domain of the eastern Arctic which represents some 20 per cent of the total land area of Canada.
It was a longstanding commitment I had made to be in Igloolik to mark this momentous occasion and to sign the agreement on behalf of the Government of Canada.
On a personal note, I want to thank the members of the community of Igloolik for their outstanding hospitality, for the warmth of the reception shown by the young children in the local school in Igloolik, the trappers who took me out on the ice floe, the hunters, the families, and especially the elders.
The hospitality and the warmth of that visit reflected joy in the face of very significant hardships and the optimism of the Inuit people of the eastern Arctic with respect to the ultimate successful implementation of this agreement and the benefits it will bring to their very remote, but very beautiful, part of Canada.
May 1, 1990

I say warmth although I must add there was no central heating in the igloo, which I had the privilege of helping to construct after midnight two nights ago and in which I slept during my stay. It was a marvellous experience that few Canadians will ever experience. I consider it a great privilege to have spent a short night sleeping in an igloo. Igloovigik they call it, an ice house.
Among the many achievements of this landmark document are the provisions for wildlife harvesting rights, participation in the management of lands and resources, and a variety of economic and cultural rights and benefits. All of these measures will ensure greater self-sufficiency for the Inuit people throughout central and eastern Arctic. This agreement will also enhance the climate in the Northwest Territories for economic and political development by removing legal uncertainty on land and resource use in the eastern Northwest Territories.
The land claims settlement will not in itself create Nunavut, which is the aspired homeland for the Inuit people, but commits the territorial government and Tungavik Federation of Nunavut to set up a mechanism for achieving a northern consensus on the division of the Northwest Territories outside the claims process. This agreement once again confirms the commitment of this government to settling comprehensive claims, to improving aboriginal relations with the federal government and building stronger native and northern economies.
I mentioned earlier that progress on this and other major claims has been achieved because of the comprehensive claims policy of this government, introduced a few years ago, and also the policy on northern political and economic development, again introduced by my predecessor who is now the Minister of National Defence. He and other ministers who preceded me laid the groundwork for the completion of historic agreements.
The agreement in principle was signed yesterday. The final agreement was signed with the Dene-Metis people three weeks ago in Yellowknife, which I had the privilege of presiding over, and four weeks ago, the historic settlement of the comprehensive claim with the Council of Yukon Indians was signed right here on Parliament
Supply
Hill in Ottawa. That too, will bring great benefit to the people of Yukon.
All across northern Canada, from the sixtieth latitude upward we now have settlements in the form of final agreements or in the most recent case, an agreement in principle with the TFN.
In the case of the Yukon settlement, approximately 7,000 Indians of Yukon are provided with over 41,000 square kilometres of land or approximately 8.6 per cent of all the land area of Yukon. They will receive $248 million in financial compensation and a share of the Yukon government's resource revenues when and if they are transferred to the territory, that is the jurisdiction over resource development. The agreement provides guaranteed participation in the management of lands, resources, fish and wildlife.
A little further to the east in the western Northwest Territories we have concluded an agreement. It was a difficult conclusion but one which was celebrated with great joy in Yellowknife three weeks ago. This agreement involves the two peoples, the Dene Indian communities of the western Arctic and the Metis who live in corresponding communities together. The Dene and the Metis work together under the leadership of Mr. Bill Erasmus and Mr. Garry Bohnet with the territorial government and the federal government to affect a successful conclusion to the Dene-Metis final agreement.
Under that agreement, the Dene and Metis peoples will receive ownership of over 180,000 kilometres of land, $500 million in compensation and a share of any future resource royalties which the government of the Northwest Territories will collect in the settlement area. As members of this House know, there are vast resources, particularly hydrocarbon resources-the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is in the House today-and very exciting and major developments afoot which, as a result of this agreement, will now be made possible.
The Dene and Metis will play a very fundamental role in the management and decision-making of the companies of that resource development. They will share in significant ways in the economic benefits that flow therefrom. Her e again there will be majority participation by the Dene and Metis people on the management

May 1, 1990
Supply
boards. They will ensure preferential hunting and fishing rights, and exclusive trapping rights for the Dene and Metis people in the region.
These comprehensive claims agreements continue a process that has been evolving for more than two centuries. These settlements are meant to clarify the rights of aboriginal and non-aboriginal peoples with respect to land and resources north of sixty. It is a way for aboriginal people to obtain lasting protection for their traditional land based interests while, at the same time, securing rights and benefits which will assist them into the next century. We will have a legal framework in which their participation in Canada and the unique recognition of their rights will be guaranteed for all time.
Above all, the settlement of these comprehensive claims lays the groundwork for new partnerships between aboriginal peoples and their non-aboriginal neighbours. Such partnerships will benefit all of Canadian society but bring special benefit to the people of the north. The traditional aboriginal respect for and understanding of the environment and its natural dynamics will be just one of the many valuable contributions they will make to Canada's future.
I want to indicate a sense of confidence in Canada and a willingness to agree, reflecting those traditional Canadian values of generosity, tolerance and respect for one another in our differences. We certainly want to see a successful conclusion to the Meech Lake Accord. It will be the conclusion of the Meech Lake Accord which allows us to move into the next and very important stage of constitutional definition involving aboriginal peoples, the stages involving the more thorough and legally binding definition of aboriginal rights and the development of structures and institutions of self-government for the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
It is the agreements which we have just concluded, and the successful conclusion of Meech Lake which will allow us to make further major and important steps toward the full delivery on the rights of native people, to have those aboriginal rights not merely named in a Constitution but become a living reality that all Canadians can better understand.
On another topic, as hon. members are aware, a number of inquiries have been held or are currently under way into the issue of aboriginal justice. A common thread that appears to be emerging from these inquiries is the necessity to adapt the justice system to the
particular needs of Indian people. Such an approach has been proposed numerous times during the initial phases of a major review undertaken by my department called the Land Revenues and Trust Review.
This review is designed to find improved mechanisms to ensure the self-administration of lands, the revenues and the rights to property by native people through a means of self-administration. When this review is completed, we believe it will constitute an important step toward effective self-government, both in treaty settlement areas and in the areas which are the beneficiaries of the new comprehensive claims and further settlements to come, especially in the province of British Columbia.
Many people believe that the only acceptable solution to the administration of justice on our reserves is to establish a justice system that recognizes the significant cultural differences that exist between Indian and nonIndian communities. Each of these alternatives, from increased use of justices of the peace to a separate Indian justice system, are being fully explored with Indian communities. In this way, we will also ensure that any changes that are made reflect the concerns of Indian communities.
If I had more time, I would like to say more about the work we are making in the new aboriginal program known as CADES, jointly with several other departments, to assist entrepreneurial development and economic opportunity for our native communities across Canada. I could speak of the implementation of Bill C-31 which brought justice to many native women who had been denied their rights to full and equal partnership and participation in the status native communities of Canada and the study that we are doing and will report to Parliament on regarding how that implementation program is going.
In conclusion, I would like to say once again that the issue of the last few days, particularly at Akwesasne, and the opportunity to debate aboriginal issues in this House in the context of aboriginal rights and justice, I think has allowed us to reflect on the tremendous amount of work that must yet be done and the awesome responsibility we have. We are all concerned about the violence and tension that has compelled some 600 Mohawk Canadian people to evacuate the village of St. Regis. My department is assisting in the adjustment and the needs of these people. We want to see them returned quickly and
May 1, 1990

in an orderly fashion to their communities where we will see peace restored.
I urge all members of the House to contribute to the wisdom and to help by suggestions of good advice as to how we might bring the parties together and involve the State of New York and the United States federal government in bringing an end to the lawlessness which has been the trigger for this very unfortunate situation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by asking the minister, perhaps as a symbolic gesture, but one which I hope he will join with me over the next few hours and days, to call upon the community of Akwesasne for calm, for understanding and compassion in what would obviously be very difficult times for them. As darkness draws near today we know what darkness has done to the days at Akwesasne. I invite the minister to join me in this symbolic gesture of wishing and perhaps praying that the people of Akwesasne will do what is right and will ensure that there is no further violence because, obviously, further violence will not contribute to peace.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could ask another question of the minister and he may want to respond to everything at once. First of all, I would like to offer perhaps a bit of a tribute to my colleagues, the member for Stormont-Dundas and the member for Beauharnois-Salaberry for their assistance, as always. Akwesasne, on the Canadian side, is partially in the riding of the member for Beauharnois-Salaberry and partially in mine. Everything that happens in Akwesasne has an effect on the riding of Stormont-Dundas as well. It is, of course, because it is right there beside it and the people of Stormont-Dundas are helping out.
I invite the minister to join me in thanking the good people of Stormont-Dundas for their assistance with the residents of Akwesasne. I want to ask the minister if he could give us any further information that he might have received this afternoon on the tragic incident of today and as well, on any progress of those meetings that his officials are having with the United States government. In particular, I ask him quite bluntly if his official has convinced Governor Mario Cuomo and his group that this problem will not go away and that this business of pretending that it is an internal Mohawk issue and that it is for Mohawks to deal with themselves is simply an inadequate proposition for anyone to entertain.

There has to be a co-ordinated approach to disarm the community of Akwesasne because there is no room in Canada or anywhere else for machine guns, AK-47s, M-16 rifles, grenades and all that other kind of thing that we see there.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the concerned and heartfelt spirit in which the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell has addressed this tragic issue.
I too, want to compliment the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry and the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas whose constituents are particularly affected by this matter. The hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry is, in particular, the member in whose riding this tragic accident occurred in Snye, in the province of Quebec.
Responding to the member's initial plea, it is for all members of Parliament to, in any way we can, have influence and to show sensitivity and wisdom, and to take recourse to our faith, because in the final analysis the resolution of this issue will only be found in the hearts of men and women who are prepared to make peace. We would all wish for a peaceful night and a peaceful few days as government officials work with the leadership of the Akwesasne Mohawk peoples to find a lasting resolution to this problem.
The problem is complicated by geographical matters relating to a border which is difficult to enforce, and jurisdictions of one state and two provincial governments. It has to do with some criminal activities which are not just restricted to organized gambling. The majority membership which elects the councils, both the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne and the St. Regis Tribal Council, as well as the traditional chiefs have tried to find a solution. In their view on behalf of the democratically elected majority, that solution would see an end to organized gambling.
The Governor of New York state, who spoke out yesterday on this issue, offered the observation that all parties should lay down their arms before some kind of mediated process could be commenced. He offered a suggestion involving one of his officials to some form of mediated process. I think it is time now to appeal to the leadership, particularly the Governor of New York, Governor Cuomo, and officials of the U.S. State Department, to work with us realizing the serious and immedi-

May 1, 1990
Supply
ate dangers of the situation, to realize that there are emotions.
There are factors relating to certain economic disparity, but also certain economic interests which go with the activities which have led to the arming of the element of the Mohawk Warriors Society, which is creating such a terrible and tragic situation. Whether realistic or not, I think it is important that another attempt be made to seek an accommodation in which the Mohawk Warriors Society is challenged to sit down, work this matter out and dispense with the violence and the use of sophisticated armaments which are merely taking their toll on people's emotions and peace of mind, and their right to security.
Just to conclude by responding to the hon. member's question, I have not had a thorough briefing as a result of the meeting that has gone on all day in the U.S. Embassy across the street between officials of the U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs and my department, under the auspices of the Department of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the U.S. Slate Department.
I have been told, however, that the discussions have focused on the means of gaining the agreement of the American authorities, that the solution to the Akwe-sasne situation requires the co-operation of all levels of government, including the American and New York state governments, and that American officials have now accepted this position, their need to be part of the solution. Furthermore, agreement was reached that an urgent meeting be arranged involving representatives of all five jurisdictions, that is; Canada, Quebec, Ontario, the U.S.A. and the state of New York. This further urgent meeting is being set up under the leadership of the federal government. More information on this meeting will be provided as soon as possible. One might ask what good are more and more meetings but meetings are the right and proper course toward peaceful settlement.
Earlier today, as I indicated during Question Period, the Canadian Embassy in Washington, Ambassador Burney I believe, approached the American State Department with a strong message of urgency, expressing our lack of satisfaction with the progress made today,
and in light of this morning's incident, the need for much more immediate, sensitive and effective action.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the minister for joining in on this debate. I do have one reservation with his comments in that I did not think he addressed the wider issue that we are facing right now. That is, that although we do have a particular crisis on one reserve, perhaps it points to the inadequacy of our judicial system relating to a lot of the native communities across this country, both urban and rural.
I wonder if the minister would like to indicate to the House to what extent that his department is willing to take the initiative in co-ordinating the Solicitor General's department and the Minister of Justice and his own department for seeing that alternative systems are developed across this country to respond more meaningfully to the problems being faced by Canadian aboriginal communities.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is speaking in the broader general spirit of his resolution so I will not link that to the Akwesasne situation which he understands is very unique and demands a very unique and special form of response.
As I tried to indicate in my broader remarks, we are seriously moving toward the development of effective forms of self- government in terms of the way in which funds are managed by native bands and by the way in which schools and services are administered and also, the way in which lands, revenues and property exchanges are administered by native leadership. We are also moving seriously in the area of forms of independent native justice systems and we have made a great deal of progress in supporting native policing.
All of this is in response to the realization by our aboriginal people that the treaties signed in the past century and in the early part of this century have not worked. We have created, through the dependency on the federal government and the provisions of the Indian Act, a situation in which they are not able to control and decide their own destiny. As a result of that we are trying to respect their desire for autonomy. That is why we do not move outside police forces or other agencies in until
May 1, 1990

we are invited to. We realize the systems in place are imperfect and I call on all members of Parliament to help us to improve them.
In the spirit of giving effective recognition to the concept of self-government we really want to respect the homelands and the communities of our aboriginal people. It is only in the face of a tragic incident like that which we are experiencing today that we realize the inadequacies of a system which has not yet had enough opportunity to demonstrate its weaknesses. As we discover the weaknesses and as we better learn to co-ordinate the efforts of government agencies in support of the needs of aboriginal people, I am sure we are going to do a much better job. We have a long way to go yet and in that sense I respect the spirit of the motion that the hon. member has put forward today.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in the House today on the motion put before us by my hon. colleague, the member for Winnipeg North Centre. I would like to add my words of condolences to the Pyke family and to the entire Akwe-sasne family who I am sure share in the loss of a brother.
The riding of Stormont-Dundas holds these people close at heart. We have been neighbours for hundreds of years and up until the last election they were members of the constituency of Stormont-Dundas. Certainly they are now ably represented by my colleague, the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. However, our ties still run very deep and very long.
It seems odd, however, that we in 1990 are debating in the House of Commons of Canada a motion which in part calls upon this House to reaffirm that all persons are equal under the law. Sadly, when it comes to the aboriginal peoples of Canada this fundamental legal right is sometimes seen, at best, as questionable and, at worst, horribly denied.
One can find several references in our country's history where aboriginal peoples have clearly not been afforded the security of Canadian law which other Canadian citizens enjoy. Moreover, there have been numerous injustices made in the past which illustrate the lack of resources and opportunities that native Cana-
Supply
dians have within our legal system. The Donald Marshall case in Nova Scotia is but one sad example.
Canadians are concerned about the state of affairs regarding our native population. We all believe in equality and we all value the rights and privileges we have. Our standard of living in Canada is one which is seen by others as being quite decent. However, when we examine the avenues open to native Canadians we see a different society, one which is lacking in the comparative opportunities of Canadian life.
Indeed, beyond the inequality in law there is a range of problems concerning aboriginal Canadians. In terms of social conditions, post-secondary education, health matters, economic opportunities, constitutional and other political rights, the aboriginal peoples of Canada have not been on the same level as most Canadians.
We also have to realize of course that if aboriginal peoples are denied the full measure of human rights and justice it should not be too surprising to find these additional inequalities in native life.
The government has dragged its feet for some time on the issue of establishing an aboriginal justice system. The government appears to be uninterested in creating this justice system. It has virtually ignored the desire of aboriginal peoples across Canada to attain self-government. This is hard to accept given that several judicial inquiries into the treatment of aboriginal peoples have submitted reports calling for such a system to be implemented.
I cannot understand the reasoning behind the government's reluctance to grant native Canadians an aboriginal justice system. My colleague, the member for Kenora-Rainy River, represents a riding which has some 46 native communities. He has personally witnessed the success of aboriginal programs and services in a manner far more beneficial and productive than government-run programs.
Surely the government must understand that the operation of a justice system by aboriginal peoples is a natural extension and that they would be able to operate it in an effective manner.
The government is once again, in my estimation, out of touch with the views of the Canadian people. As far back as April, 1989, a telephone research survey asked the question: "Should the native people have the right to law

May 1, 1990
Supply
enforcement, trial and punishment for offences committed, on native lands?" Nationally, 73 per cent of respondents said yes; in Ontario 89 per cent agreed likewise. In every province a majority of respondents were in favour of an aboriginal justice system.
Still the government of Canada has failed to move ahead and reflect the wishes of Canadians on this matter.
In a letter dated November 20, 1989, to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development Grand Chief, Michael Mitchell of the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne clearly outlined the need for an aboriginal justice system. In discussing the problems on the Akwesasne reserve, Chief Mitchell wrote: "In times of potential violence it is human nature for people to look for signs of continued stability and progress from their leaders. Therefore, it is crucial for the Mohawk Council to demonstrate this stability and progress. In order to do this we need the co-operation of the federal and provincial governments".
Chief Mitchell was simply pointing out an obvious fact, that it is sensible and reasonable to suggest that aboriginal leaders are best able to understand what is required for their particular communities.
Chief Mitchell made this point very clear to the minister in a brief accompanying his letter. In referring to the Akwesasne judicial system, Chief Mitchell wrote: "As the governing body, the Mohawk Council is answerable to the Mohawk people of Akwesasne for all decisions which affect their daily lives". That being the case, I certainly believe that no aboriginal council within any native community would take their responsibilities to their people lightly.
Aboriginal leaders would not make legal decisions affecting their people on their own. Chief Mitchell writes that their council is constantly receiving advice from their people on how to handle local matters. However, when the council acts on these recommendations they find they are up against a brick wall with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
According to Chief Mitchell, out of necessity and established procedure, an accepted law by his council is sent to Indian Affairs where it is usually rejected. The
basis for this rejection is part of the over-all problem. In Chief Mitchell's assessment: "Government officials sitting at a desk far from Akwesasne cannot possibly know of the background information or circumstances prompting the passing of a law".
There are several circumstances for aboriginal leaders to invoke laws in their communities. It is impossible for bureaucrats who only look at the drafted law to see the reasons for such a law or the conditions which exist in the community. According to Chief Mitchell, these laws are usually rejected without consultation with his council. In the past four years, Chief Mitchell indicates that 14 council laws have been disallowed by the federal government. Most of these had to do with protecting the community from illegal activities brought into the reserve from the outside. These rejections do not help the relationship between the aboriginal leaders and Indian Affairs.
We have another problem here and that concerns the antiquated Indian Act. In a brief sent to all members of Parliament in April, the Native Women's Association of Canada states that the Act's very title "evokes feelings and actions that have caused anguish, pain and suffering to Indian people for well over 200 years and it continues".
The association points out that while the rest of the country takes pride in its growth and prosperity, the original peoples of this land continue to suffer needlessly as a result of legislation which affects aspects of native life from birth to death.
In terms of justice, the Mohawk Council of Akwesasne believes the interpretation of the Indian Act is so narrow in scope that the laws passed for Akwesasne cannot be sanctioned by the federal government. In the opinion of Chief Mitchell, such a situation limits the legal capacity of the Mohawk Council to regulate activities within Akwesasne and is contradictory to the process of selfgovernment. Most would also come to the conclusion that the Indian Act is as bad for self-government and aboriginal justice as it is for the protection of aboriginal human rights.
It is clear that an aboriginal justice system would alleviate a good portion of the problems caused to some degree by the injustices of the Indian Act. Unfortunately, the present government does not see this. It seems more content to express vocal concern about native self-government and the ever-pressing need for an
May 1, 1990

aboriginal justice system, but never seems to get around to implementing it.
Unfortunately, native Canadians continue to suffer. They are denied full access to human and legal rights and self-determination. The current state of native life in Canada does not present a vibrant, promising picture. Life on reserves is increasingly difficult. Native leaders and their councils are unable to adequately govern in their communities. They are restricted by an Indian Act which is badly in need of change while at the same time having to cope with a number of negative socio-economic issues.
It is also difficult to make do with the policies and programs thrown to them by a federal government which has no commitment and no vision for the future of aboriginal peoples.
I have no doubt at at all that the present crisis on the Akwesasne reserve may well have been avoided, if the Mohawk people on both sides of the border had the rights and opportunities as those afforded to most citizens in both countries.
It is important that this House reaffirm its support and commitment to aboriginal human rights and equality under the law. I know that members will indeed want to convey to our native population that they are willing to support a system of justice which is suited to their particular needs and aspirations. It is imperative, however, that the government start to show leadership in creating aboriginal justice initiatives and assist in the development of such a system in consultation with native leaders across the country. We have an opportunity to correct past wrongs and implement necessary changes which will create a better future for the aboriginal peoples of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and speak to this motion introduced by my colleague for Winnipeg North Centre which is the adjacent constituency to my riding of Winnipeg North. I thank my colleague from Stormont-Dundas for sharing his time with me.
The motion states:
That this House reaffirm that all persons are equal under the lawand demand that the government (1) promote this fundamental human right for Canada's aboriginal peoples, (2) ensure that our system of justice is more responsive and suitable, (3) pursue alternative
Supply
aboriginal justice initiatives, and (4) in cases of jurisdictional conflict,
that the Government of Canada, in consultation with aboriginal
leaders, ensure the protection of the life, liberty, and security of
aboriginal people who are entitled to the status of Canadian citizens.
This motion sends twin messages from Parliament to the government that the government reaffirm equality under the law and demand that this equality be fulfilled; that the law should recognize no class, colour, creed or origin when it treats citizens and that, moreover, the law should recognize the inherent dignity of all human beings.
This principle is embodied in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Why then do we have to reaffirm it in the motion of today? Because we recognize that there is a threat to, a weakness in and, in some instances, actual failure of our Canadian justice system.
The evidence for this failure has been alluded to by my colleagues who have spoken earlier: the Betty Osborne murder in The Pas, Manitoba, that went unsolved for more than a decade; the J.J. Harper killing in Winnipeg as a consequence of prejudgment by our police department; and the Donald Marshall wrongful imprisonment in Nova Scotia. All these injustices reflect the continuing struggle that native people continually face in our country.
We have all heard of or seen the conditions endured by the great majority of Canada's native people. Most reserves in isolated communities have experienced great difficulties in developing an economy capable of sustaining their growing populations. The results are tragic. We have witnessed for them high levels of unemployment, welfare, violence, suicide and alcoholism.
It appears that political self-determination and economic self-sufficiency for them are almost unreachable goals. We have to understand that aboriginal peoples want their culture, traditions and pride back.
The situation of the First Nations' people has been likened to that of blacks in South Africa. I do not think the analogy is accurate or fair. The fact, however, that it is made at all speaks volumes about this aspect of Canada's international profile.
Let me quote from a letter dated March 28, 1990 from Phil Fontaine of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs to the Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission: He stated:

May 1, 1990
Supply
The Canadian Government is perceived internationally, as a strong advocate of Human Rights, as is the case with its high profile role in support of the Black struggle for independence in South Africa. It is often a source of financial support to Third World Countries. It speaks out against Human Rights abuse in other countries. Through these gestures, Canada has gained a strong international reputation as a staunch defender of human rights. This is in sharp contrast domestically with its relationship with First Nations people.
That is the assessment by the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs.
Even the United Nations Human Rights Commission has examined the allegations of treaty violations in Canada. How can we respond to such a situation? One way is to re-examine certain aspects of these relations. For example, the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs is just beginning a review of the government's comprehensive claims policy. Yet this review alone is not enough. This policy is only one aspect of the complex relationship between Canada and some native peoples. Many government services to native people are not even addressed by these claims; Metis and non-status Indians are not even addressed by that policy. There is considerable disillusion with the claims themselves. For example, the Cree of northern Quebec are arguing that the claim they negotiated should be declared null and void due to non-compliance by the federal government.
Let me quote from the 1988 report of the Commissioner of the Canadian Human Rights Commission. He said:
Surely, one supposes, in a country like Canada, it is not possible that an entire group of people should, in the 1990s, be so remote from sharing in the benefits that others take for granted. Surely, with all the money and effort that are lavished on the problem, it ought to be amenable to solution. Once again, however, the unpleasant fact of the matter is that it has not been, and that it still shows only rudimentary signs of being resolved.
The time for piecemeal approaches to such a complex situation of the first peoples of our country has passed. In fact, when you look at the 1990 report, Unfinished Agenda for all Canadians in the 1990s, of the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs, it has addressed 30 issues, from land claims to literacy.
The time has come for the Government of Canada to establish a national royal commission on aboriginal peoples, to consolidate all previous reports on this issue, to examine the remaining relevant issues on a broader
perspective, and to offer realistic solutions-to correct the tragic and the continuing tragic situations for our aboriginal people.
About a year ago, I put on the Order Paper a resolution to this effect. Of course, it has not yet had a chance to be put forward for debate. I thought I should seize this opportunity to speak about the need to establish a royal commission on this issue. This has been echoed by the major media, like The Globe and Mail, in our country. This royal commission should examine all aspects of the relationship between the Government of Canada and the native peoples of this land. It should recognize the many strengths of native communities and successes of government policy as well as the weaknesses and failures. It should look to the future as well as acknowledge the past and, above all, it should hear the thoughts and aspirations of the native peoples themselves.
In 1987, on the occasion of the visit to Canada of His Holiness Pope Paul II, a headline in the Toronto Star, September 21, 1987, read: "Let Canada be a model to the world for the rights of native people", and he continued, "For a just and equitable degree of self-governing, with the land base and adequate resources necessary for the development of a viable economy for present and future generations". He called on Canada to ensure the basic aboriginal rights, including self-government.
My former leader, the Right Hon. John Turner, as quoted in the Toronto Star the following day stated:
MPs should act on the Pope's message by amending the Meech
Lake accord to include regularly scheduled constitutional
conferences on native self-determination.
"Aboriginal peoples cannot wait indefinitely".
The royal commission can serve as an instrument for national self re-examination, reconciliation and unity. It could serve as a tool for achieving consensus, to raise the profile of the issues to the Canadian consciousness and thereby achieve the desired changes. This royal commission may well serve as the milestone in the rebirth of native peoples in Canada, as a cornerstone of new relationships between the aboriginal and non-aboriginal peoples of our country.
In conclusion, I would like to quote briefly from the report of the Standing Committee of our Parliament in March this year, An Unfinished Agenda for all Canadians in the 1990s which stated:
May 1, 1990

The circle of Confederation will not be complete until the social, the
economic and political marginalization of Canada's aboriginal people
is reversed.
The report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission indicated that a national Royal commission could play a useful role in achieving consensus without being used as an excuse for delaying important practical developments.
In the years ahead, our success in forging a new association between the aboriginal and the non-aboriginal Canadians will be the prime nature of our commitment to equality and our skill in nation building and, at the very end, we can relive the message of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 200 years ago: "All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights". Let us make our native people equal with all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have 15 minutes left. I therefore would like to ask the unanimous consent of the House for sharing my speaking time with my colleague here behind me, who would like to speak to the same subject. If you agree, I will take four or five minutes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I want to thank the House for its understanding at this tragic moment.
First of all, I would like to join the entire community on the Akwesasne reserve in offering my sincere condolences to the family of Matthew Pyke who died this morning. When I say family, I am aware that on reserves, the meaning of the word family differs from my own because it also includes Grand Chief Mike Mitchell with whom I often had the honour and the privilege of working, and I realize how deeply affected they must be at this moment on the reserve.
Mr. Speaker, this morning's casualty occurred in my riding. I should explain that the Akwesasne Indian Reserve is divided into three parts: one part is in Quebec, in my riding; one part is in the riding of my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, and the third part is in the United States. I cannot remain unmoved by these events, because I have often acted to defend the rights of people who asked for help on the
Supply
reserve, and I think it is often brought home more strikingly when we have tragic events such as those occurring today.
From my riding of Beauharnois-Salaberry, if I want to visit people in the reserve that is located in my riding, I have to go through the United States and come back via Ontario to finally get there. Mr. Speaker, there are personal problems and physical problems on the reserve. There are physical problems that once solved could probably help us deal with the human problems, because considering what is happening along the border, we could probably have organized an effective patrol if we had a land link that would have allowed us to go directly from our side to the territory that is on the Canadian side of the border.
Mr. Speaker, at the end of March, I found it very moving-my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell was also invited but he could not attend that morning-when I went to St. Lawrence College in Cornwall where a program was launched in which the federal government invested about $600,000, which came from the budgets of the Department of Employment and Immigration and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I am referring to the Mohawk Law and Security Program. I saw about thirty students who said they were ready to continue their education and were in fact taking courses in communications, defence, law, American law and Canadian law. I saw a chief, Mike Mitchell, and at the time it surprised me to see a chief who was broken, not morally, but a man who was getting a lot of threats and who told me that morning, in public: This may be my last public appearance as chief.
Fortunately, he changed his mind, but this man is now under terrific pressure and is receiving a lot of threats.
I think Chief Mike Mitchell, like Jean-Guy Hudon or anyone else in this House, has a right to want to live in peace and develop his community on the basis of principles he holds dear, principles that run very deep among the first inhabitants of this riding.
Do I have the right to intervene, Mr. Speaker? I certainly do. And I have that right because these are people from my riding, people whom I have never denied assistance, whom I have never turned down. Personally, I think this is a tragedy, and I would urge the departments to co-ordinate their operations and especially to show our U.S. neighbours that there are problems in this

May 1, 1990
Supply
respect and that we must find a solution. What is happening to Mike Mitchell, to the people in my community and to those in the riding of Glengarry- Prescott-Russell is probably due to the fact that government authorities cannot agree on what to do and are afraid to intervene.
The other day I had an unfortunate experience because people wanted to establish a nuclear waste site right near the Canada-U.S. border. I intervened, and people said: "You know, you don't put a nuclear waste site in a national park. But it isn't dangerous. You don't put it in a reserve. It isn't dangerous".
It's funny how careful people are when a reserve is concerned, when we should intervene, we are excessively prudent, and when a chief like Mike Mitchell asks for help, we may be in less of a hurry to do so because there is the human factor. And there are some very serious examples of this at work right now.
I strongly urge this government and this House to intervene as quickly as possible and explain to our neighbours to the south that any intervention should be co-ordinated, effective and respect the values dear to our friends living on the reserve, and ensure that these people will be able to live and prosper within their own territory.
Mr. Speaker, I yield immediately to my colleague who certainly has a few things to add on the subject.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to rise in the House today to speak to the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
In the last few months that I have been in the House, I have had the privilege of serving on the justice committee and also on the aboriginal affairs committee. In view of what is happening in the last few months with respect to the justice inquiries that have been held, I think it is particularly timely today to be talking on this issue.
The fundamental freedoms of our aboriginal peoples, and other members of Canadian society, are protected by the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The charter clearly identifies and guarantees basic human rights, and provides a means of redress to the courts
should these rights be denied or infringed by governments.
Among the rights enshrined by the charter that may be considered of particular importance to our native peoples are the right to worship in a manner, place and time that one chooses, and the freedom to pursue activities and goals in association with others.
Another key protection enshrined in the charter is the right to be equal before and under the law and the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination on any ground, including race, national or ethnic origin, and colour.
Moreover, the equality guarantee in the charter is expressly phrased so as not to preclude laws or programs designed to favour individuals or groups who may be at a disadvantage in society. Such laws or programs could, of course, include native people and numerous government programs are structured to provide affirmative action for aboriginal peoples.
The charter has also been successfully employed to protect the livelihood of native people who rely on hunting as a way of life. For example, in the Chief case, a mandatory five-year prohibition on possession of firearms for conviction of a weapons offence was held by the Yukon Territory Court of Appeal to be cruel and unusual punishment, contrary to the charter, in the case of aboriginal people. The court recognized that the effect of the mandatory prohibition on possession of firearms for an aboriginal person who relied on trapping could result in the deprivation of that person's livelihood and lifestyle. Accordingly, in light of the totally debilitating effect that the prescribed punishment would have had on the aboriginal accused, the court altered the sentence.
Mention must also be made of Section 25 of the Charter, which specifically protects aboriginal concerns. This section makes clear that no other provision of the Charter can be used in a way that will interfere with any special rights that the native people have now or may acquire.
For example, any new benefits aboriginal people may gain from a settlement of land claims would not run afoul of the general equality rights as set out in the Charter. As well, Section 35 of the Constitution Act 1982, states that the existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are recognized and affirmed.
May 1, 1990

Both of these sections were possible only after very considerable work by aboriginal people like those of the Four Nations of Hobbema. These provisions, and others, were written into the Canadian Constitution specifically at their request and of other native organizations. Representatives of these groups argued forcibly for recognition that would help their people preserve their culture and identity, customs, traditions, languages and treaty rights.
Rights without any means of redress would be empty, so the Charter provides that any person whose rights or freedoms have been infringed or denied may obtain a remedy from the courts. The federal government, recognizing that without financial assistance, deserving individuals or groups may not be able to challenge federal legislation or practices in the courts, has established a special fund to assist litigation of important equality issues. The Court Challenges Program has a budget for litigation and legal research, plus administration funds over five years, and is administered by a private non-profit organization. To date native groups have benefited from this fund.
In summation, I think it should be clear that the Charter offers protection to aboriginal groups. These groups have used the Charter to challenge government policies and to enforce native rights. This is the way it should be. The Charter is a document that we, as Canadians, should be proud of. It reflects our heritage as a just society, as well as our continued respect for fundamental human values.

Mr. Speaker, I rose in the House some time ago to protest the cuts affecting women's centres. I put a number of questions to the Secretary of State, and I am not very satisfied with the answers, because it seems that whenever we ask him why he cut subsidies for women's centres, he always says he increased the subsidies. Actually, it seems we have a communications problem and I will explain why.
First of all, we know that in some programs, money is always available for women to set up certain projects. We are not challenging the funding for various projects but the way women's centres are being attached by cutting core funding, in other words, money for ongoing activities. This is a very serious problem because when groups such as women's centres, consumer associations or any other non-profit association have ongoing activities and funding is cut for those activities, the government is actually controlling these organizations, Mr. Speaker.
Personally, as a former president of an association that was often obliged to ask the government for subsidies, I was often in a situation where governments said: Listen, we can't give you the money for hydro and rent and basic needs, but we can give you all kinds of subsidies for small projects. All kinds of small projects. Meaning that we, the government, can give you the money for any project we are willing to approve.
I imagine that in the case of a women's centre, this has a destabilizing and even destructive impact because you spend all your time trying to get subsidies for various projects. This means you have keep justifying the fact that you need money. You are leading a hand-to-mouth existence. And the people you hire will only be there for the duration of the project. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, if you, as Speaker of the House, were given a contract for three months. Would you have agreed to be here for just three months? Of course not. I think that, like any reasonable

May 1, 1990
Adjournment Debate
and intelligent person, you would have sought longer-term employment. At least, I think so.
That is the problem with the cuts to the women's centres. It is demoralizing for the women's centres, as for any group, and it forces them to always ask the governments for money; they are even forced to offer programs or projects that suit the governments but that may not be so suitable for the community or be in tune with its needs.
So, Mr. Speaker, I hope that this time the government will understand me. It will also understand, I hope, why the women are fighting. The 75 women's centres across the country, and especially the 39 women's centres in Quebec, are not just protesting the cuts. It is not just that.
Please do not say that you gave a lot of money yesterday. Yes, you gave some, you made a lot of money available to them for projects. But I am not talking about that.
I am talking about core funding, the grants for ongoing activities.
And now I will ask you to be a little more sensitive to our requests. I am new here in the House of Commons and I always believed that people on both sides, in the government and the opposition, were reasonable.
So I appeal to your reasonableness and if you want proof that what I am saying to you is correct, before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I will quote you an excerpt from a letter by someone who sits for the government, who is even a minister of the government. I am talking about the hon. Minister for International Trade, that great defender of women's rights, that great friend of the member for Hamilton East. He himself said-he even wrote a letter-

I want to say what the minister wrote in English. It is very short, Mr. Speaker, and I will conclude with that because I find it tells the government, from a member of the government, what the position is.
The minister wrote to the Secretary of State complaining about the decision to cut funding for 75 women's centres across the country and asked that every possible effort be made to keep the centres open. He said
specifically: "I can assure you that the women of Newfoundland and Labrador will suffer desperately without these centres and since the cut to core funding for women's centres in Newfoundland is only $240,000 and the national figure amounts to only $1.6 million, it is hard to believe that money is the real issue here".

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for his question. I believe it was on April 10 that he put his question to the Secretary of State. At that time he was referring mainly to the women's centres in his own home province so the answer that I have prepared is more specifically related to his home province than to the total question on which he has elaborated tonight.
In his own home province the Quebec provincial government has committed to improving the social welfare of women in the province and that government must be commended for the action that it has taken.
The budget for women's centres of the provincial Ministry of Health and Social Affairs was more than $800,000 in 1988-89. Last August the Quebec government increased the funding for women's centres to $2.7 million by the end of the 1992 fiscal year.
This is a fine example of a provincial government taking on its responsibilities. That is the point. The core funding for the centres are a provincial responsibility and that is why the minister is working with regard to the project funding. This is a fine example of how a provincial government can work with the federal government during a time of economic restraint to sustain programs that are vital to the health of our country.
The government is well aware of the excellent work carried out in women's centres. Along with the support provided by the Quebec government and other provincial governments through their funding for services, the Department of the Secretary of State is making project funding available to centres that previously had received core funding to carry out education activities.
Project funding can be used to address issues such as family violence, pornography, sexual assault, employment equity and other concerns. Along with provincial funding, the Secretary of State has assured women's

May 1, 1990

Adjournment Debate
centres that they will be eligible for funding for the administrative costs related to the project activities.
So, Mr. Speaker, the Government of Quebec has recognized the absolute necessity of having strong women's centres in that province. I hasten to add that Manitoba has also shown provincial leadership in this area. There are four women's centres in that province and each receives approximately $115,000 of annual funding from the provincial government.
This government is living up to its fiscal responsibilities, not only for Canadians today but for the future generations as well. Financial responsibility does not mean that essential services must disappear. With the co-operation of the provinces all of us, as a nation, can work together to ensure that women's centres are able to continue to play their important role in Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, on March 26 I asked the Minister of the Environment to explain why this government has failed to involve itself in the fight to eradicate aquatic milfoil weed in the interior lakes of southern British Columbia. I did not get a very satisfactory answer at that point, Mr. Speaker, and that is why I am back here at this time.
The Eurasian milfoil weed, scientifically called Myri-phyuum Spicatum, is a very rapidly growing aquatic weed species that has infested many of the lakes and rivers in the interior of the province of B.C. It is because of its growth rate and its ability to actually regenerate when it has been fragmented, for example, by boat propellers, that it has proliferated to such an extent and has choked off many recreational areas and now, in fact, threatens to invade many of our salmon bearing streams and rivers.
I will read a very brief excerpt from the October 1989 edition of the British Columbia Report. It says:
The province's latest battle with milfoil has forced its small army of milfoil combatants into retreat and has prompted local governments in the Shuswap area to admit defeat. All this despite a -campaign to stomp out the proliferate water weed. Ttvo regional districts and the provincial government were involved in the fight, but even their best efforts weren't enough to root out the spindly foe.
This uncontrolled growth of the milfoil weed poses a serious environmental threat as well as a serious economic threat. The Okanagan and the Shuswap Lakes watersheds rely very heavily on clean lakes for their tourism industry. The overgrowth of this particular weed is already costing the local tourist industry in the Okanagan and Shuswap area valuable business as tourists go elsewhere rather than deal with the clogged propellers and the beaches that have been strewn with rotting weeds.
In 1985 tourists brought over $287 million to the Okanagan region and spent about 80 per cent of their time on the beaches. Recent market studies have shown that a growing number of these tourists are in fact going elsewhere, having become very concerned because of the deteriorating quality of the lakes.
Swimming, boating and fishing certainly are not the only things that are affected by the proliferation of this weed. The thick weed carpet acts as a filter and traps garbage and sediment which settles on the lake bottom and interferes with normal water flows and the ecological balance of those lakes.
Despite their years of effort, the North Okanagan Regional District, as well as the Columbia Shuswap Regional District, have been fighting essentially a losing battle with this nuisance weed.
At this point nature has, at least for now, conquered man in the Shuswap and she holds the upper hand in the South Okanagan where the weed has virtually taken over the Okanagan River. It has threatened Kokanee salmon and is running rampant in Vaseaux Lake near Oliver where it first appeared in 1981.
In Shuswap Lake to the north there is great concern that commercial houseboats may in fact be carrying the weed into nearby lakes and rivers. In Woods Lake, Kalamalka Lake, Skaha Lake and Okanagan Lake, all throughout the interior, thousands of hectares of waterfront have been spoiled with the growth of this weed.
In 1989 a survey of Shuswap Lake showed a 20 per cent increase in the weed growth from the previous year, even with the control efforts, with new infestations appearing on Seymour Arm and right in the main body of Shuswap Lake.

May 1, 1990
Adjournment Debate
The regional districts and the provincial governments are losing ground in the milfoil battle. The Columbia-Shuswap Regional District has recently passed a resolution requesting federal assistance in this battle to control this aquatic weed species. I think I can safely say that the resolution has the full support of the North Okanagan Regional District as well as the Okanagan Basin Water Water Board and local councils.
The fact of the matter is that the time has come for federal involvement in this environmental and economic crisis. The 1987 federal water policy, I might remind you, commits this government to a co-operative approach to water management problems with the various provinces. The policy emphasizes an integrated approach to water management that can only be construed as a direct involvement in such environmental issues in concert with the provinces and the regions of those provinces.
The Minister of the Environment, while expressing interest in the milfoil problem when I brought it up on March 26, was characteristically vague in what action he would take. In talking to the minister after the debate in the Chamber here, he indicated that after his Green Plan was announced he would like his advisers to meet with me on that very issue. Well that was over a month ago and I am still waiting.
I would like to ask the minister's representative who is going to be answering shortly whether the Minister of the Environment at this time, or in the immediate future, will meet with myself and my colleagues, the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt. All three of our ridings are directly involved with this very critical issue. Would he meet with us as a delegation to discuss specifically what actions he and his ministry are prepared to take regarding this very, very serious environmental concern that essentially affects the entire interior portion of British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member opposite for clearly stating the problem in our British Columbia lake system. I am quite familiar with it because it is my home province as well.
He quite correctly stated that we did put a water policy out in 1987 which stated that the federal government would co-operate with provincial governments in co-operative management of water resources. He knows, too, that under the Constitution Act, the provinces exercise direct control over many aspects of water management. As the overview to the federal water policy states, the federal government intends to work in conjunction with the provinces and territories to encourage the provision of safe and sufficient water supplies for Canadians in areas of federal and shared responsibilities.
The federal government policy incorporates two main goals. The first is to protect and enhance the quality of the water resource. This means that the federal government will work to anticipate and prevent contamination of Canadian water supplies by harmful substances introduced through pollution and to encourage the restoration of waters that are already contaminated. We are realizing this goal by developing and, as in the case of the British Columbia, implementing such programs as joint water monitoring agreements. The second goal is to promote the wise and efficient management and use of water, meaning that new ground rules must be established that respect the value of water to all sectors of society and to the environment.
The infestation of which the member opposite speaks in the interior of British Columbia lakes by Eurasian water milfoil as with lakes in other parts of Canada, has been of concern since the early 1970s. The federal government has devoted considerable time, effort and money to try and solve the problems generated by this weed. Its propogation is not brought about by increased water pollution or the deterioration of water quality, but by the aggressive way it grows once it enters a lake. The problems caused by this weed are primarily related to recreation and tourism, to aesthetics and to access to swimming beaches, rather than to the quality of the water itself.
The responsibility for actual weed control operations rests with provincial and local governments. There are existing cost-shared programs for aquatic weed control between the B.C. Ministry of Environment and local authorities such as the Columbia-Shuswap Regional District and the Okanagan Basin Water Board. This mechanism-

speechtext:
I hear the hon. member. Everybody wants more money and the federal government is not what you would call flush with money.
I think that what is taking place has been working quite well as far as the money goes. Relief is provided at the highest priority for the recreational areas.
The federal government continues to play an important role in both liaison and technology transfer with the province of British Columbia by its participation on the federal-provincial B.C. Aquatic Weed Advisory Committee. As well as Environment Canada, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is also active on that committee. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans has funded and undertaken research studies in Cultus Lake, B.C.-which is in my riding-to assess the value of Eurasian milfoil as habitat for juvenile fish. By contrast, the effect that infestations of this weed have on fish habitat is not yet known.
The infestation in the lakes of the interior of British Columbia by Eurasian milfoil, as with the lakes in other parts of Canada, has been of real concern and continues to be of real concern.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me this opportunity this afternoon to seek clarification from the Minister of Transport with respect to a question I asked him some weeks ago in this House.
On April 2 I questioned the minister about the inefficient and unsafe conditions at Pearson International Airport. More specifically, asked about the relationship between the statements he had made in several instances to this House and how they did not confirm the report of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board that was issued on the date that the Canadian Aviation Safety Board was disbanded.
The question was not a difficult one. It dealt with several of those recommendations. I asked the minister specifically what he intended to do with respect to the 48 recommendations that were made by the Canadian Aviation Safety Board that date and what type of timeframe the minister was proposing with respect to
Adjournment Debate
their implementation. I asked that mainly because some of the recommendations of the very thorough, in depth study made by the safety board required some immediate implementation.
What I received was, in essence, almost no reply. I would almost think that the minister did not not want to reply because of the very unsafe and inefficient conditions that exist at Pearson International Airport at the present time.
The questions I asked were confirmed by the report to which I have been referring. Simply, why was there, in the year just ended, a 66 per cent increase in the number of near-misses in the southern Ontario airspace from the previous year? That is a pretty simple question. Why are we having more near-misses in the airspace around Pearson today than we had a year ago?
What is really happening at Pearson Airport with respect to the efficiency of that airport? Why is there such a slowdown in the operations and services they are providing?
More important, we have heard in this House on many instances reference to the air traffic controllers. Why is the morale among the air traffic controllers at Pearson International Airport so low? What is happening with those people in that position of such great responsibility? Why are they not more enthused about doing the job? Thank goodness they are dedicated people in that profession who have mainly the safety of the travelling public as their goal.
Why do different departments, airside and groundside, not appear to operate co-operatively and effectively in the administration of the Pearson Airport?
The Speaker of the House and I were both in Pearson airport. He was coming from Vancouver and I was coming from Thunder Bay and we were both sitting in the airport waiting for the plane to Ottawa when there was a security breach and one of the alarms went off. The question I asked, which has still not been answered, and which I will continue to ask in this House, is why it took 15 and a half minutes for the RCMP to respond to that breach of security at Canada's largest airport. When they did respond they could not give any logical reason, and I explored it in full detail, why it took them 15 and a half minutes to respond.

I am trying to ask the Minister of Transport, through you Mr. Speaker and through the House, for the benefit of all Canadians who use our airspaces, why these conditions are allowed to exist at Pearson International Airport.
In essence those are the questions I would like my friend across to answer this afternoon. I know that we are under some time restraints. If I could get some assurance that those questions would be answered this afternoon, I would be prepared to sit down right now and rely on his answers. Let me conclude and give him the opportunity to answer those questions. I hope he will take all of the time that is still available to me and the time that is available to him to respond.
I am not catching him off guard. My hon. friend was at a transport committee meeting with me just a short while ago and I told him I was going to use some comparisons as I was asking this question this afternoon. As he said to the previous speaker, he is from the Province of British Columbia. We know that the airport in Vancouver is perhaps one of the most efficient airports in the whole of Canada and it faces much the same problems as Pearson faces on a day-to-day basis. It has almost as many flights. In fact, propeller driven aircraft and helicopters at Vancouver airport far exceed those at Pearson.
For the benefit of all Canadians who use these airports, why do we not adopt at Pearson the good management philosophies that we are using at the Vancouver airport in his province? That is fairly simple and it would solve the problems that we are experiencing at Pearson.
With that, Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity of asking those questions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman opposite makes it all sound so very simple. I wish it were. However, the member opposite has a continuing interest in what is happening at Pearson airport because he has a vital interest in air safety and air traffic in Ontario.
The report that he talked about, the Canadian Aviation Safety Board's report on air traffic, which did make 48 recommendations for improving the Canadian system,
should not be interpreted as 48 deficiencies within the system at Lester B. Pearson International Airport.
As mentioned, the recommendations made by the CASB pertain to the entire system, some of which are related to technology now in the research and development stage, while others require international agreement and participation in the area providing control over the high seas.
The CASB recommendations can be implemented quickly. Indeed, the majority already have been. I can assure the hon. member that all recommendations have been given the utmost attention.
As part of that, as an ongoing procedure, the minister did put together a task force on aviation matters. In fact, it was such an important matter that my colleague, the Minister of Transport, established a task force in order to seek the expertise of the private sector, the industry and the government. The aim of that task force was to ensure that we have the right resources and that they are used in the right way in order to meet the changing needs of the future.
Speaking more specifically of Toronto, as we all know, Toronto is our busiest airport in Canada. The air traffic controllers have a difficult job which they do well. As the member knows very well, we are working to improve the situation at Toronto. We have hired former American controllers. We have increased the number of training seats available. There has been a cap on airline movements per hour at Toronto which will not be removed until the minister is satisfied that traffic can be handled safely and efficiently.
I can assure the hon. member that Toronto is still being actively studied to make sure that it is able to fill its role in the airline and transportation industiy of this country.
